chapters.n: The book opens with a title linking it to Solomon, David’s son, famed for the wisdom God gave him. The book itself shows later collections were added (Hezekiah’s scribes, Agur, Lemuel), so “Solomon” heads the whole anthology.

f.g: Hebrew mashal—a short saying, comparison, or parable that packs truth into a memorable line.

chapters.n: Verses 2–6 state the book’s purpose. It is meant to help readers gain wisdom (skill for living well), accept correction, and understand wise teaching.

f.g: Hebrew ḥokmah—practical skill in living, the know-how of a craftsman applied to life and righteousness.
Hebrew musar—discipline, training, or correction, like a parent shaping a child.

chapters.n: Wisdom here isn’t just cleverness. It includes moral qualities: doing what is right, fair, and honest toward others.

f.g: equity = fairness, uprightness; treating people evenly.

chapters.n: Proverbs is especially written for the inexperienced and the young, to give them good sense before life tests them.

f.g: subtilty = shrewdness, prudence—here a good quality: the ability to see through traps.
The naive or inexperienced—someone easily led, not yet set in either wisdom or folly.

chapters.n: Proverbs is not only for beginners. Even the wise grow wiser by listening, and those who understand can gain skill in guiding their lives.

f.g: Literally “steering”—the skill of a sailor guiding a ship.

chapters.n: The book will teach how to understand proverbs, riddles, and deep sayings. Wisdom literature often makes the reader think hard to unlock its meaning.

f.g: dark sayings = riddles or puzzling sayings that need thought to understand.

chapters.n: This is the motto of the whole book. True knowledge begins with reverence for the Lord. Refusing that foundation is what makes someone a “fool” in Proverbs—a moral, not mental, failure.

f.g: Reverent awe, trust, and obedience toward Jehovah.
Hebrew ʾevil—a person who is morally stubborn and refuses correction, not merely unintelligent.

chapters.n: The first lecture begins. A father addresses his son, but both parents teach. In Israel, family instruction was the first school of faith.

f.g: A teacher’s affectionate address to a student or child; it appears often in Proverbs 1–7.

chapters.n: Parents’ teachings are like a lovely garland on the head and a necklace—something that adorns and honors the one who wears it.

f.g: A graceful wreath or garland worn on the head.

chapters.n: A short, firm warning: when sinners try to lure you in, just say no. The rest of the passage shows how persuasive such invitations can be.

f.g: entice = lure, persuade with tempting promises.

chapters.n: The father quotes the gang’s pitch: let’s ambush someone innocent just because we can. The violence is planned and unprovoked.

f.g: privily = secretly; to hide and wait in ambush.

chapters.n: The gang brags they will swallow their victims whole, like the grave (Sheol) swallows the dead. They imagine themselves as powerful as death itself.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the realm of the dead.
Another name for the grave or the world of the dead.

chapters.n: Their real motive is greed: easy riches and houses full of loot. Crime is sold as a shortcut to wealth.

f.g: spoil = plunder, loot taken by force.

chapters.n: The final hook is belonging: join us, share our common fund. Peer pressure offers friendship and equal shares.

f.w: Cast in thy lot among us
f.g: Throw in with us; join our group and share its fortunes.

chapters.n: The father’s answer: don’t even start down that road with them. Avoiding the first step is the surest protection.

f.w: refrain thy foot from their path

chapters.n: Their feet are fast to do harm. Isaiah used nearly the same words, and Paul quoted them to describe human sinfulness.

A puzzling proverb. One likely meaning: a bird that sees the net being spread will avoid it—so you, warned in advance, should avoid this trap. Another reading: even birds aren’t that foolish, yet these men are.

f.w: in vain the net is spread
f.g: A fowler’s net was useless if the bird watched it being set.

chapters.n: The irony: the ambush they set for others is really an ambush for themselves. Violence destroys the violent.

f.w: they lay wait for their own blood

chapters.n: The lesson of the story: greed for dishonest gain ends up taking the life of the very person who grasps it.
A new speaker appears: Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman preaching in public. Unlike the gang lurking in secret, Wisdom speaks openly to everyone.

f.g: without = outside, in public places.

chapters.n: She goes where crowds gather—the busiest streets and the city gates, where business and court cases took place. Wisdom is available to anyone who will listen.

f.g: The noisiest, busiest spot where people crowd together.
City gates were the ancient town square, where elders judged cases.

chapters.n: Wisdom asks three kinds of people “how long?”: the naive who enjoy being naive, mockers who love to mock, and fools who hate knowledge.

f.g: scorners = mockers, scoffers who ridicule correction and holy things.

chapters.n: Wisdom’s invitation: turn around when I correct you, and I will pour out my spirit and teach you. Repentance opens the door to revelation.

f.w: I will pour out my spirit unto you

f.g: reproof = correction, rebuke.

chapters.n: Wisdom has called repeatedly and held out her hand like someone beckoning, but no one paid attention.

f.w: I have stretched out my hand

chapters.n: They treated her advice as worthless and wanted none of her correction.

f.g: set at nought = treated as nothing, disregarded.

chapters.n: Strong poetic language: when disaster comes, Wisdom will “laugh.” The point is not cruelty but that those who mocked wisdom will find their mockery turned back on them.

f.w: I also will laugh at your calamity

chapters.n: Disaster is pictured as a sudden storm or whirlwind. The consequences of ignoring wisdom often arrive all at once.
In crisis they finally call, but too late. The warning is that refusing wisdom over and over can leave a person without it when they need it most.

f.g: early = eagerly, diligently.

chapters.n: The reason is clear: they chose this. They hated knowledge and refused to reverence the Lord. Wisdom respects human agency.

f.w: did not choose the fear of the LORD

chapters.n: A summary restatement: they wanted none of Wisdom’s counsel and despised her correction.

f.w: They would none of my counsel

chapters.n: The principle of natural consequences: they will eat the fruit of the path they chose. People are “filled” with their own schemes.

f.w: eat of the fruit of their own way

f.g: devices = schemes, plans.

chapters.n: Wandering from wisdom kills the naive, and the careless ease of fools ruins them. Comfort without wisdom can be deadly.

f.g: Their careless ease or complacency.

chapters.n: The chapter ends with a promise: whoever listens to Wisdom will live securely and be at peace, free from dread.
This chapter is one long “if…then” sentence in Hebrew. The “if” begins here: if you take my words to heart and treasure my commands like something valuable you store away.

f.g: Store them up like treasure.

chapters.n: Seeking wisdom involves both listening (the ear) and caring deeply (the heart). In Hebrew thought the heart is the center of thinking and choosing, not only feeling.

f.g: Lean in and listen closely.

chapters.n: Wisdom must be wanted. The seeker cries out for understanding like someone calling desperately for help.
Search for wisdom the way miners dig for silver or treasure hunters search for buried gold—with effort and persistence.
The “then” arrives: if you seek wisdom like that, you will come to understand reverence for the Lord and actually come to know God.
Wisdom is ultimately a gift. Human effort seeks it, but the Lord gives it. Both sides matter.
The Lord stores up wisdom for the upright and is their shield.

f.g: buckler = a small shield.
Real, effective wisdom that succeeds.

chapters.n: God watches over the paths of justice and protects the way of his faithful ones.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim—faithful, loyal ones.

chapters.n: Another “then”: the seeker will understand what is right, just, and fair—every good road in life.
The key moment is when wisdom moves from outside instruction to inner delight—when it enters your heart and you enjoy it.

f.w: knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul

chapters.n: Good judgment becomes a bodyguard, watching over you from within.

f.g: discretion = good judgment, thoughtful prudence.

chapters.n: Wisdom’s first rescue is from evil men and their twisted talk.

f.g: froward = perverse, twisted, contrary to what is right.

chapters.n: These men deliberately leave straight paths to walk in darkness. The image of two paths—light and dark—runs through Proverbs.

f.w: walk in the ways of darkness

chapters.n: Worse than doing evil is delighting in it—enjoying the perverse ways of the wicked.
Their roads are crooked and their paths devious—the opposite of the straight path of wisdom.
Wisdom’s second rescue is from the “strange woman”—the adulteress—who uses smooth words. This warning returns in chapters 5–7.

f.g: Literally a woman who is a “stranger” to you—another man’s wife or a woman outside the covenant; here an adulteress.

chapters.n: She has abandoned the husband of her youth and broken the marriage covenant made before God. Marriage is described as a sacred covenant, not just a contract.

f.g: Her husband, the companion of her youth.

chapters.n: Her house slopes downward toward death. Adultery is pictured as a road that leads to spiritual and physical ruin.

f.g: Hebrew rephaim—the shades, the departed spirits of the dead.

chapters.n: Those who go to her don’t easily come back to the path of life. The warning shows how hard it is to recover from such a choice.

f.w: None that go unto her return again

chapters.n: Wisdom’s goal is positive: to keep you walking with good people on righteous paths.
The upright will live in the land. For Israel, dwelling in the promised land was the sign of covenant blessing.

f.w: the upright shall dwell in the land

f.g: perfect = whole, blameless, of integrity.

chapters.n: The contrast: the wicked will be uprooted from the land like a weed. The chapter ends with the two destinies side by side.
The father asks his son not just to remember his teaching but to keep it in his heart—obedience that comes from within.

f.g: Hebrew torah—teaching or instruction, here a parent’s guidance.

chapters.n: Living by wise teaching tends to bring long life and peace. Proverbs states general principles of how life usually works, not guarantees for every case.

f.g: Hebrew shalom—wholeness and well-being, not just absence of conflict.

chapters.n: Keep loyal love and faithfulness close: wear them like a necklace and write them on your heart like a tablet. The image recalls the law written on stone, now written inward.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed and ʾemet—steadfast covenant love and faithfulness.
table = tablet, a writing surface.

chapters.n: The result is a good reputation with both God and people—just as was said of the boy Jesus.

f.w: in the sight of God and man

chapters.n: One of the best-loved verses in the Bible. Rely on the Lord completely, rather than relying only on your own limited judgment.

f.w: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart

f.g: Do not prop yourself up on; don’t put your full weight on.

chapters.n: Recognize God in every part of life, and he will make your road straight—clearing the way and guiding you to the right destination.

f.g: Literally “know him”—stay aware of him and seek his will.
Or “make your paths straight.”

chapters.n: Don’t be impressed with your own cleverness. Humility before God and turning from evil are the start of real wisdom.

f.w: Be not wise in thine own eyes

chapters.n: Humble obedience is pictured as medicine for the body—healing to the core and refreshment to the bones.

f.g: Likely “body” or “flesh” in the original; the core of one’s physical self.

chapters.n: Honor God with your possessions, giving him the first and best of what you earn. Firstfruits were the first part of a harvest offered to the Lord.

f.g: substance = wealth, possessions.

chapters.n: The promise attached to generous giving: overflowing barns and wine vats. Latter-day Saints often connect this with blessings promised for tithing.

f.g: Winepresses or vats where grape juice was collected.

chapters.n: Don’t resent the Lord’s discipline or grow tired of his correction. Hard experiences can be part of God’s training.

f.g: chastening = discipline, corrective training.

f.w: despise not the chastening of the LORD

chapters.n: God disciplines because he loves, like a father who delights in his son. The book of Hebrews quotes this to comfort struggling believers.

f.w: whom the LORD loveth he correcteth

chapters.n: A new section praises wisdom itself. “Happy” here means truly blessed or fortunate.

f.g: Hebrew ʾashre—blessed, fortunate; the same word that opens Psalm 1.

chapters.n: Wisdom is a better investment than silver or gold. Its profits last.

f.w: better than the merchandise of silver

chapters.n: Wisdom is more precious than rubies (or red corals)—nothing you could want compares to her.

f.g: Possibly red coral or pearls; the exact gem is uncertain, but it means something very costly.

chapters.n: Wisdom is pictured as a woman offering gifts in both hands: long life in one, riches and honor in the other.

f.w: Length of days is in her right hand

chapters.n: Wisdom’s roads are pleasant and all her paths lead to peace.
Wisdom is a tree of life—recalling the tree in Eden. Latter-day Saints may think of Lehi’s vision, where the tree of life represents the love of God.
God used wisdom to found the earth and set the heavens in place. Chapter 8 will expand this picture of wisdom present at the Creation.

f.w: The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth

chapters.n: By God’s knowledge the deep waters burst forth and the skies give dew—water above and below sustains life.

f.g: In dry Israel, dew was a vital source of moisture for crops.

chapters.n: Keep wisdom and good judgment in view; don’t let them slip out of sight.

f.g: Practical, effective wisdom.

chapters.n: Wisdom gives life to the soul and is like a beautiful ornament around the neck.
With wisdom you walk safely and don’t trip—a picture of a steady, secure life.
Wisdom brings peace even at night: you lie down unafraid and sleep well.
Don’t panic at sudden terror or at the ruin that comes on the wicked.
The secret of fearlessness is the Lord himself: he is your confidence and keeps your foot out of the hunter’s snare.

f.g: Caught in a trap, like an animal in a snare.

f.w: the LORD shall be thy confidence

chapters.n: Practical neighborly duties begin here. If you can help someone who deserves it, do it. Withholding good is a real wrong.
Don’t put off a neighbor with “come back tomorrow” when you can help today. Delay can be a form of unkindness.
Don’t plot harm against a neighbor who trusts you and lives peacefully beside you. Betraying trust is especially wicked.
Don’t pick fights with someone who has done you no wrong.

f.g: strive = quarrel, contend, bring a dispute.

chapters.n: Don’t envy violent people, even when they seem to succeed, and don’t copy their methods.
The Lord detests the devious, but he shares his confidence with the upright—his “secret” means close friendship and counsel.

f.w: his secret is with the righteous
f.g: secret = intimate counsel, close fellowship.
abomination = something God finds detestable.

chapters.n: A contrast of two homes: the house of the wicked lies under the Lord’s curse; the home of the righteous is blessed.

f.g: habitation = dwelling, home.

chapters.n: God mocks the mockers but gives grace to the humble. Both James and Peter quote this verse (from the Greek Old Testament).

f.w: he giveth grace unto the lowly

chapters.n: The wise will inherit honor; fools only get “promoted” to disgrace. The chapter ends contrasting two outcomes.
The father now speaks to all his children, inviting them to pay attention so they can gain understanding.

f.g: attend = pay close attention.

chapters.n: He assures them his teaching is good and worth holding onto. A parent’s instruction is offered as a gift, not a burden.

f.g: doctrine = teaching, what is received by learning.

chapters.n: The father remembers his own childhood: he too was once a tender, cherished son. If Solomon is the speaker, this recalls David and Bathsheba, though the passage could fit any father.

f.g: Young, delicate, and especially dear—“only” can mean uniquely loved.

chapters.n: He quotes what his father taught him. Wisdom is passed down generation to generation—each parent teaching what they themselves received.
The grandfather’s words continue: acquire wisdom and understanding, and never drift away from them.

f.g: “Get” means acquire or buy, as in a purchase.
decline = turn aside, drift away.

chapters.n: Wisdom is pictured as a faithful companion who will guard you if you stay loyal to her and love her.
Wisdom is the most important thing. Whatever it costs, even all you have, get understanding.

f.g: Or “The beginning of wisdom is: get wisdom!”
With all you possess—spend everything if needed.

chapters.n: If you prize wisdom highly, she will raise you up and bring you honor when you hold her close.

f.g: Prize her, value her highly.

chapters.n: Wisdom crowns the one who loves her with a beautiful wreath and a crown of glory.
The father returns to his own voice: listen, and you will have a long life.

f.w: the years of thy life shall be many

chapters.n: He has guided his son in the straight paths of wisdom—now the son must keep walking in them.

f.g: Straight, level paths.

chapters.n: On the path of wisdom, you have room to move and can even run without tripping.

f.g: straitened = narrowed, hemmed in, restricted.

chapters.n: Grip instruction tightly and never let it go, because it is your very life.

f.g: Hold firmly, cling.

chapters.n: Don’t even step onto the road of the wicked.

f.w: Enter not into the path of the wicked

chapters.n: Four quick commands pile up for emphasis: avoid it, don’t go near it, turn away, keep moving. The best way to resist temptation is distance.
The wicked are so addicted to doing harm that they can’t sleep until they’ve caused someone to fall.

f.g: mischief = harm, evil (stronger than the modern meaning).

chapters.n: Wickedness and violence are their daily bread and wine. What they live on is what they become.

f.g: Food gained by wickedness, or wickedness as their constant diet.

chapters.n: A beautiful image: the life of the righteous is like dawn, growing brighter and brighter until full noon. Spiritual growth is gradual and increasing.

f.g: The full brightness of midday.

chapters.n: The wicked walk in deep darkness and don’t even know what makes them stumble.

f.w: they know not at what they stumble

chapters.n: A new lesson begins with the familiar call to listen carefully.

f.g: Lean your ear toward—listen closely.

chapters.n: Keep these words both in sight and deep in your heart.

f.w: keep them in the midst of thine heart

chapters.n: Wise words bring life and health to the whole body. Spiritual wholeness and physical well-being are connected in Proverbs.

f.g: Or “healing for their whole body.”

chapters.n: Guard your heart above all else, because everything in your life flows out of it. In Hebrew, the heart is the center of thoughts, desires, and choices.

f.w: Keep thy heart with all diligence
f.g: Or “above all that you guard.”
issues = springs, sources, outflowings.

chapters.n: After the heart, the mouth: get rid of twisted, dishonest speech.

f.g: froward = crooked, perverse.

chapters.n: Next, the eyes: look straight ahead and keep your focus on the goal, not on distractions.
Then the feet: think carefully about where you are walking, and your path will be steady.

f.g: Or “make level, smooth.”

chapters.n: Don’t swerve right or left; keep your foot away from evil. Heart, mouth, eyes, and feet—the whole person must stay on the path.

f.w: Turn not to the right hand nor to the left

chapters.n: The father begins a lesson on sexual morality, calling his son to listen closely.

f.g: Lean in and listen carefully.

chapters.n: The goal is that the son will keep good judgment and speak with knowledge rather than be led by smooth talk.

f.g: discretion = careful judgment, thoughtful planning.

chapters.n: The adulteress’s words seem sweet as dripping honey and smoother than olive oil. Temptation always looks attractive at first.

f.g: An adulteress—a woman outside one’s marriage covenant.

chapters.n: But the aftertaste is bitter and the outcome cuts like a sword. Sin promises sweetness and delivers pain.

f.g: wormwood = a very bitter plant, a symbol of bitterness and sorrow.

chapters.n: Her path leads straight down to death and the grave.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: She never thinks about the path of life; her ways wander and she doesn’t even know it. Her life is unstable and aimless.

f.g: Her ways wander, unsteady and shifting.

chapters.n: The father pleads again with all his children to hold on to his words.

f.w: depart not from the words of my mouth

chapters.n: The best defense: stay far away. Don’t even go near her door.

f.w: come not nigh the door of her house
f.g: nigh = near.

chapters.n: Adultery can cost your honor and the best years of your life, handing them to people who will show no mercy.

f.g: Possibly an angry husband or others who exploit the offender.

chapters.n: Strangers may end up enjoying the wealth you worked for. Infidelity brings real financial and family costs.

f.g: The fruits of your hard work.

chapters.n: At the end of life, the man who chose this path groans as his body wastes away—perhaps through disease or simply in old-age regret.

f.g: Or “groan.”

chapters.n: His regret is spoken aloud: why did I hate correction and despise warnings?
He admits he refused to listen to those who tried to teach him.

f.g: Listened attentively.

chapters.n: He came close to complete ruin in front of the whole community—public disgrace was one of the consequences.

f.g: The gathered community, possibly where cases were judged.

chapters.n: Now the positive side: find joy in your own spouse. Water from your own cistern and well is a poetic image of marital love.

f.g: cistern = a stone-cut tank for collecting rainwater—precious in a dry land.

chapters.n: A rhetorical question in many translations: should your springs overflow into the streets? The meaning is that your love should not be scattered abroad.

f.w: Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad
f.g: Many translators read this as a question: “Should your springs be scattered abroad?”

chapters.n: Keep your love for your spouse alone, not shared with strangers.

f.w: Let them be only thine own

chapters.n: May your marriage be blessed. Rejoice in the wife you married when young—fidelity is meant to be a source of joy, not just duty.

f.w: rejoice with the wife of thy youth

chapters.n: Frank and tender poetry celebrates married love. The doe and gazelle were images of grace and beauty. God intends husband and wife to delight in each other.

f.g: hind = a female deer, a doe.
roe = a gazelle or small deer.
ravished = captivated, intoxicated with delight.

chapters.n: So why be captivated by another man’s wife? The question shows how foolish it is to trade a faithful love for a forbidden one.

f.w: embrace the bosom of a stranger

chapters.n: Nothing is hidden. The Lord sees every path a person takes and weighs every step.

f.w: before the eyes of the LORD

f.g: pondereth = weighs, examines carefully.

chapters.n: The wicked get trapped by their own sins, tied up as if by ropes. Sin binds the one who commits it.

f.g: holden = held.

chapters.n: He dies because he refused discipline, staggering off course in his great foolishness.

f.g: Hebrew word also used in verse 19 for being “ravished”—a wordplay: captivated by folly instead of love.

chapters.n: First of four short lessons: don’t rashly co-sign for someone else’s debt. Shaking hands was how such a pledge was made.

f.g: surety = one who guarantees another’s debt, like a co-signer.
Struck hands—a handshake that sealed a binding agreement.

chapters.n: Your own words have trapped you. A rash promise can catch you like a snare.

f.g: snared = caught in a trap.

chapters.n: The fix is urgent humility: go to the person, swallow your pride, and plead to be released from the pledge.

f.g: Press your friend hard; keep pleading with him.

chapters.n: Don’t sleep until you have resolved it—this is serious and needs immediate action.

f.w: Give not sleep to thine eyes

chapters.n: Escape like a gazelle from a hunter or a bird from a trapper—with all your energy.

f.g: roe = gazelle.
fowler = a bird-catcher.

chapters.n: Second lesson: laziness. The lazy person is told to learn from the tiny ant.

f.g: sluggard = a lazy person, a habitual idler.

chapters.n: The ant has no boss watching her, yet she works anyway. Self-motivation is part of wisdom.
She stores food in summer and harvest time, preparing for winter. Planning ahead is wise.

f.g: meat = food in general.

f.w: gathereth her food in the harvest

chapters.n: The father mockingly asks the sluggard how long he plans to lie there.
The sluggard’s excuse, quoted: just a little more sleep. Small delays add up.

f.w: a little folding of the hands

chapters.n: Poverty will arrive like a traveling robber or an armed raider—suddenly and unstoppably.

f.g: Like a vagabond or highwayman who comes unannounced.
want = need, lack.

chapters.n: Third lesson: the troublemaker. He is worthless and wicked, going about with crooked talk.

f.g: Hebrew “man of belial”—a worthless, good-for-nothing person (much stronger than modern “naughty”).

chapters.n: He communicates with secret signals—winks, foot movements, finger gestures—to deceive or conspire.
His heart is full of perversity; he is always scheming harm and stirring up conflict.
His disaster will come in an instant, and he will be shattered beyond repair.

f.g: Without healing; beyond fixing.

chapters.n: Fourth lesson: a list of what the Lord hates. “Six… yea, seven” is a Hebrew number pattern that builds to a climax on the last item.

f.g: The “x, x+1” pattern draws attention to the final item in the list.

chapters.n: Arrogant eyes, a lying tongue, and murderous hands. The list moves through parts of the body, showing how sin can take over the whole person.
A heart that plots evil and feet that hurry to do harm—sin starts inside and then moves into action.
A false witness and one who stirs up strife among family or community. The seventh item—sowing discord—is the climax: God especially hates breaking apart people who should be united.
The father returns to his main theme: keep your parents’ teachings.

f.w: forsake not the law of thy mother

chapters.n: Keep these teachings always close, bound on your heart and around your neck. The language echoes the command to bind God’s word on hand and forehead.

f.w: Bind them continually upon thine heart

chapters.n: These teachings act like a guide in the daytime, a guard at night, and a counselor in the morning—with you at every moment.
God’s commandment is a lamp and his teaching is light; even correction is a road to life.
These lessons especially protect against the smooth talk of the immoral woman.
Don’t let desire for her beauty grow in your heart, or let her capture you with fluttering eyes. Jesus taught the same: sin begins with the heart and eyes.

f.w: Lust not after her beauty in thine heart

chapters.n: A prostitute may cost a man his last loaf of bread, but an adulteress hunts his very life. The second is far more dangerous.

f.g: Reduced to poverty, down to a crust.
The very life or soul of a person.

chapters.n: A vivid question: can you carry fire against your chest without your clothes catching? Some actions carry unavoidable consequences.

f.g: bosom = chest, the fold of a garment over the chest.

chapters.n: Or walk on hot coals without burning your feet? Of course not.
Likewise, the man who sleeps with his neighbor’s wife cannot escape guilt or punishment.

f.g: Will not go unpunished.

chapters.n: People may feel some sympathy for a thief who steals because he is starving.

f.g: soul = appetite, life; to satisfy his hunger.

chapters.n: Even so, he must repay heavily—possibly everything he owns. Theft has a price that can be paid back.

f.g: “Sevenfold” means full, complete repayment.

chapters.n: Adultery is worse: it shows a lack of sense and destroys one’s own soul. Unlike stolen goods, the damage cannot simply be repaid.

f.g: Literally “lacks heart”—has no sense.

chapters.n: He will be wounded and disgraced, and the shame will be very hard to erase.

f.g: reproach = disgrace, public shame.

chapters.n: A betrayed husband’s jealousy burns like fury; he will show no mercy when he seeks justice.

f.w: jealousy is the rage of a man

chapters.n: No payment or gifts will satisfy him. Unlike theft, adultery cannot be bought off.

f.g: ransom = a payment to settle a wrong or buy release.

chapters.n: The father opens his final warning about immorality by urging his son to treasure his teachings.

f.g: Store them up like treasure.

chapters.n: Guard these teachings as carefully as you protect the pupil of your eye—the most sensitive and precious part.

f.g: The pupil of the eye; something guarded instinctively and with great care.

chapters.n: Tie them on your fingers as a reminder and write them on your heart. The outward reminder and the inward commitment go together.

f.g: table = tablet.

chapters.n: Make wisdom your sister and understanding your close relative. If wisdom is your family, you won’t be drawn to the false intimacy of the seductress.

f.g: kinswoman = female relative; close family member.

chapters.n: Wisdom’s purpose is protection from the smooth-talking adulteress.
The father tells a story like a parable, as if he watched it happen from his window.

f.g: casement = window lattice, a latticed opening.

chapters.n: He sees a naive young man among a group of youths, one lacking sense.

f.g: Literally “lacking heart”—without good sense.
Naive, easily influenced people.

chapters.n: The young man wanders near her corner and heads toward her house. He isn’t forced; he drifts into temptation’s neighborhood.
Time passes from dusk to deep night. Darkness suggests both the hour and the moral setting.

f.w: in the black and dark night

chapters.n: A woman meets him dressed like a prostitute, with a cunning, guarded heart.

f.g: subtil = crafty, cunning; her heart is guarded and scheming.

chapters.n: An aside describes her: loud, defiant, restless—she never stays at home.

f.g: stubborn = rebellious, defiant.

chapters.n: She is always out—in the streets, in the squares—waiting at every corner. Temptation actively hunts.
She grabs him, kisses him, and speaks with a brazen face.

f.g: impudent = shameless, brazen, bold.

chapters.n: She cloaks sin in religion: she has offered peace offerings and has meat from the sacrifice at home. Peace-offering meat had to be eaten quickly, giving her a reason to invite him to a feast.

f.g: Sacrifices whose meat was shared and eaten by the worshipper within a day or two.
Fulfilled a vowed offering.

chapters.n: She flatters him: she came out looking specifically for him. He is made to feel chosen and special.

f.g: Eagerly looking for you in particular.

chapters.n: She describes her luxurious bed covered with expensive imported fabrics from Egypt.

f.g: Egyptian linen was a prized luxury import.
decked = spread, covered, adorned.

chapters.n: She has scented it with exotic perfumes. Every detail appeals to the senses.

f.g: Costly imported spices and perfumes.

chapters.n: Her invitation is blunt: let’s indulge ourselves all night.

f.g: solace = comfort, take pleasure.

chapters.n: She assures him there’s no risk—her husband is away on a long trip.

f.g: goodman = the man of the house, the husband.

chapters.n: He took money and won’t be back until a set time, like the full moon. She promises secrecy and safety—both false.

f.g: Possibly “the day of the full moon,” a set date.

chapters.n: Her flood of persuasive words wins him over. Flattery can overpower a weak will.

f.g: Smooth, persuasive talk.
She pushed or compelled him—overpowered his resistance.

chapters.n: He follows her at once, like an ox led to slaughter or a fool to punishment. He has no idea what awaits.

f.g: straightway = immediately.
A device for restraining a prisoner; the Hebrew here is difficult.

chapters.n: He rushes like a bird into a trap, not knowing it will cost him his life—until an arrow pierces his vitals.

f.w: a dart strike through his liver
f.g: dart = arrow; the liver stood for the vital center of life.

chapters.n: The father turns from the story to apply it: children, listen carefully.

f.g: hearken = listen and obey.

chapters.n: Don’t let your heart drift toward her ways, and don’t wander onto her paths.

f.g: decline = turn aside.

chapters.n: She has brought down many victims, even strong men. No one is too strong to fall to this temptation.

f.w: many strong men have been slain by her

chapters.n: The sobering ending: her house is a highway to the grave, down into the rooms of death.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, the place of the dead.

chapters.n: In contrast to the seductress lurking in the dark (chapter 7), Wisdom calls out openly. Wisdom here is personified as a woman who speaks for herself.
She stands on high ground and at the crossroads, where everyone can hear her.

f.g: Where the roads meet—the crossroads.

chapters.n: She calls at the city gates and doorways, the busiest public places in an ancient town.

f.g: The gate area was the town’s marketplace and court.

chapters.n: Her message is for everyone—all humanity, not just a select few.

f.g: All people, all humankind.

chapters.n: She especially invites the naive and the foolish to gain sense. No one is beyond her invitation.
What she offers is noble and right.

f.g: Noble, princely things.

chapters.n: Wisdom speaks only truth; wickedness is detestable to her.
Nothing she says is twisted or crooked.

f.g: froward = crooked, perverse.

chapters.n: Her words are clear to anyone with discernment and right to those who have found knowledge.

f.g: plain = straightforward, clear.

chapters.n: Choose her teaching over silver and knowledge over the best gold.
Wisdom is worth more than precious gems; nothing you could want compares to her.

f.g: Possibly red coral or pearls—something very costly.

chapters.n: Wisdom lives with prudence and knows how to plan well. In KJV English, “witty inventions” meant clever, discerning plans—not jokes.

f.g: witty = wise, skillful; “inventions” = plans or discretion. Shrewd, thoughtful planning.
prudence = shrewd good sense.

chapters.n: Reverence for the Lord includes hating evil. Wisdom names what she hates: pride, arrogance, evil conduct, and perverse speech.

f.w: The fear of the LORD is to hate evil

chapters.n: Good counsel, sound judgment, insight, and strength belong to Wisdom.
Rulers govern well and make just laws through wisdom. Solomon himself had asked God for wisdom to rule.
All leaders—princes, nobles, and judges—need wisdom to lead justly.

f.w: all the judges of the earth

chapters.n: Wisdom loves those who love her, and those who seek her earnestly will find her.

f.w: those that seek me early shall find me
f.g: early = earnestly, diligently.

chapters.n: Wisdom offers lasting riches and honor—wealth joined with righteousness.

f.g: Lasting, enduring wealth.

chapters.n: What wisdom produces is better than the finest gold and silver.

f.g: revenue = yield, income, return.

chapters.n: Wisdom walks in the path of righteousness and justice.

f.g: judgment = justice.

chapters.n: She endows those who love her with real wealth and fills their storehouses.

f.g: substance = real wealth, what truly exists and lasts.

chapters.n: The poem’s high point begins: Wisdom was with the Lord before creation. Many Christians have seen here a foreshadowing of Christ, the Word who was with God in the beginning.

f.g: Hebrew qanani—“acquired,” “possessed,” or “brought forth” me; translators differ.

f.w: in the beginning of his way

chapters.n: Wisdom was established from eternity, before the earth existed. Latter-day Saints may recall that intelligence and truth are eternal.

f.w: I was set up from everlasting

chapters.n: Before oceans and springs existed, Wisdom was already there.

f.g: The deep waters of the primeval ocean.

chapters.n: Before mountains were set in place and hills were formed, Wisdom was brought forth.
Before God had made the land, fields, or even the first specks of soil.

f.w: the highest part of the dust
f.g: Perhaps “the first of the dust”—the earth’s first particles.

chapters.n: When God laid out the heavens and drew a circle on the face of the deep—marking the horizon—Wisdom was present.

f.g: compass = circle, boundary—like the horizon drawn over the sea.

chapters.n: When God set the clouds in place above and made the deep springs strong.
When God set limits for the sea and laid the earth’s foundations. Creation is pictured as an orderly act of a wise Builder.

f.w: that the waters should not pass his commandment

chapters.n: Wisdom was beside God like a master craftsman or a beloved child, delighting before him every day.

f.w: as one brought up with him
f.g: Hebrew ʾamon—either “master workman” or “little child/darling”; scholars debate which.

chapters.n: Wisdom rejoiced in the inhabited world and especially delighted in humanity. Creation was made with joy, and people were the crown of it.

f.w: my delights were with the sons of men

chapters.n: Wisdom’s appeal: since she was there at creation and knows how the world works, listen to her. Those who follow her ways are blessed.

f.w: blessed are they that keep my ways

chapters.n: A simple command: listen to instruction, become wise, and don’t reject it.
The blessed person is like an eager visitor who waits at Wisdom’s door every day, hoping to be let in.
To find Wisdom is to find life and the Lord’s favor. Christians hear an echo of Christ, who said he is the life.
Rejecting Wisdom harms the rejecter. Those who hate her are, in effect, choosing death.

f.w: all they that hate me love death

f.g: Or “misses me”—the Hebrew word for sin means to miss the mark.

chapters.n: Chapter 9 contrasts two hostesses inviting guests to two feasts. Wisdom has built a sturdy, beautiful house with seven pillars—seven suggesting completeness and perfection.

f.g: Seven often symbolizes completeness; a grand, well-built house.

chapters.n: She has prepared a rich banquet: meat slaughtered, wine mixed with spices, and the table set.

f.g: Mixed wine, often with spices or water, for a feast.

chapters.n: She sends out her servant girls and calls from the highest points of the city.

f.g: maidens = young servant women.

f.w: upon the highest places of the city

chapters.n: Her invitation is to the naive and those lacking sense—exactly those who need her most.

f.g: wanteth = lacks.

chapters.n: Come eat my bread and drink my wine. Christians may hear an echo of Christ’s invitation to the bread of life and the sacrament.
Leave foolishness behind and live; walk in the way of understanding.

f.g: Or “leave simpleness behind.”

chapters.n: A brief interlude on teaching: correcting a mocker only brings you insult and abuse.

f.g: A stain or injury—abuse thrown back at you.

chapters.n: Don’t waste correction on scoffers—they’ll hate you. But correct a wise person and they will love you for it. How we respond to correction reveals our character.

f.w: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee

chapters.n: Teach the wise and righteous and they will grow even wiser. Learning builds on learning.
The theme of the whole book returns: reverence for the Lord is where wisdom starts, and knowing the Holy One is true understanding.

f.w: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom

f.g: Hebrew plural, often understood as “the Holy One”—God himself.

chapters.n: Wisdom speaks again: through her your days will be lengthened.
Each person reaps their own choices. Wisdom benefits you; scoffing hurts you alone. This stresses personal responsibility.
Now the second hostess: Folly, pictured as a loud, ignorant woman.

f.g: clamorous = loud, noisy, unruly.

chapters.n: She sits in her doorway on a seat in the city’s high places—copying Wisdom’s location to compete with her.

f.w: a seat in the high places of the city

chapters.n: She calls to passers-by who are minding their own business, trying to pull them off their straight path.

f.g: passengers = passers-by, travelers on the road.

chapters.n: Her invitation uses the exact words of Wisdom’s (verse 4). Temptation often imitates the good to deceive.

f.w: Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither

chapters.n: Folly’s menu: stolen water and secret bread—the thrill of the forbidden. Her feast offers only what is stolen, while Wisdom offers a real banquet.

f.g: Often understood as a metaphor for illicit sexual pleasure.

chapters.n: The guest doesn’t realize her house is full of the dead—her past guests are in the depths of the grave. The two invitations lead to life or to death.

f.g: Hebrew rephaim—the shades, departed spirits.
Hebrew Sheol—the grave, realm of the dead.

chapters.n: A new collection begins (chapters 10–22:16): short, two-line sayings, most contrasting the wise and the foolish. The first is about family: a child’s choices bring joy or grief to parents.

f.g: A heading that starts the main collection of individual sayings.
heaviness = grief, sorrow.

chapters.n: Wealth gained by wickedness has no lasting value; righteousness is what truly saves.
The Lord will not let the righteous go hungry, but he pushes away the cravings of the wicked.

f.g: suffer = allow, permit.
famish = go hungry, starve.

chapters.n: Lazy hands lead to poverty, but hard work brings wealth—a general principle of everyday life.

f.g: A lazy, careless hand.

f.w: the hand of the diligent maketh rich

chapters.n: A sensible young person works hard during harvest; one who sleeps through it brings shame. Some opportunities only come at certain seasons.
Blessings rest on the righteous person’s head, but the mouth of the wicked hides violence.

f.w: violence covereth the mouth of the wicked
f.g: Their words conceal violent intentions.

chapters.n: The righteous are remembered with blessing; the name of the wicked rots away and is forgotten.

f.w: The memory of the just is blessed

chapters.n: The wise welcome instruction, but a babbling fool comes to ruin.

f.g: prating = chattering, babbling foolishly.

chapters.n: Integrity gives a secure path; crooked dealings eventually come to light.

f.g: Walks securely, without fear.
Will be found out, exposed.

chapters.n: A sly wink—a sign of deceit—causes trouble, and the babbling fool falls. The second line repeats verse 8; sayings were sometimes reused in different collections.

f.w: He that winketh with the eye

chapters.n: The words of the righteous refresh others like a spring of fresh water; the words of the wicked hide violence.
Hatred stirs up quarrels, but love covers over offenses. Both Peter and James echo this teaching.
Wisdom is heard on the lips of the discerning, but a rod is needed for the one without sense.

f.w: a rod is for the back

chapters.n: The wise store up knowledge, but a fool’s mouth invites disaster.

f.g: Treasure it, store it for later use.

chapters.n: An observation, not a moral judgment: wealth protects the rich like a fortified city, while poverty leaves the poor vulnerable.

f.g: A fortress—wealth acts as a protective wall.

chapters.n: The earnings of the righteous lead to life; what the wicked gain leads to more sin.

f.g: tendeth = leads toward.

chapters.n: Accepting discipline keeps you on the road to life; refusing correction leads others (and yourself) astray.

f.g: erreth = goes astray, or causes others to go astray.

chapters.n: Hiding hatred behind lies and spreading slander both mark a fool.
The more you talk, the more likely you are to sin. Holding your tongue is wise.

f.g: refraineth = holds back, restrains.

chapters.n: A righteous person’s words are as valuable as fine silver; the thoughts of the wicked are nearly worthless.

f.g: Refined, pure silver.

chapters.n: The righteous nourish many with their words, but fools starve for lack of sense.

f.g: Like a shepherd feeding a flock.

chapters.n: The Lord’s blessing brings real wealth without the trouble that often comes with riches gained other ways.

f.w: he addeth no sorrow with it
f.g: Or “hard toil adds nothing to it.”

chapters.n: A fool enjoys wrongdoing like a game, but a person of understanding delights in wisdom.

f.g: sport = fun, a game.

chapters.n: What the wicked fear will happen to them; what the righteous long for will be given.

f.w: the desire of the righteous shall be granted

chapters.n: The wicked are swept away like a passing storm, but the righteous stand firm forever. Jesus told a similar parable of the wise and foolish builders.
A lazy messenger is as irritating as vinegar on the teeth or smoke in the eyes.

f.g: Those who send him on an errand.

chapters.n: Reverence for the Lord tends to lengthen life; wickedness tends to cut it short.
The hope of the righteous ends in joy, but the expectations of the wicked come to nothing.
The Lord’s way is a refuge for the upright but ruin for evildoers.

f.g: Or “a stronghold, a refuge.”

chapters.n: The righteous will never be uprooted; the wicked will not remain in the land.
The mouth of the righteous produces wisdom like a fruit tree; a perverse tongue will be cut off like a barren branch.

f.g: Literally “bears fruit, sprouts.”

chapters.n: The righteous know what words are fitting; the wicked speak only what is twisted.

f.g: frowardness = perversity, twistedness.

chapters.n: Merchants weighed goods on balance scales. Rigging the scale or using a false weight cheats people, and God detests it; honest weights delight him. Business ethics are spiritual matters.

f.g: Stones of standard weight used to measure silver or goods.

chapters.n: Pride leads to disgrace, but humility brings wisdom.

f.w: When pride cometh, then cometh shame

chapters.n: Integrity guides honest people like a compass, but crookedness destroys the treacherous.

f.g: Hebrew tummah—wholeness, being complete and undivided.

chapters.n: Riches can’t save anyone on the day of judgment; only righteousness can.
The righteousness of the blameless makes their road straight; the wicked trip over their own wickedness.

f.g: Makes his path straight and smooth.

chapters.n: Righteousness rescues the upright, but the treacherous are trapped by their own evil desires.

f.g: naughtiness = wickedness, evil craving (stronger than modern usage).

chapters.n: When a wicked person dies, all their hopes die with them. Their plans were built only for this life.
The righteous are rescued from trouble, and the wicked fall into it in their place—as happened when Haman was hanged on his own gallows.

f.w: the wicked cometh in his stead

chapters.n: A godless person destroys neighbors with words, but knowledge rescues the righteous.

f.g: Hebrew ḥanef—godless, profane person.

chapters.n: A whole city celebrates when good people prosper and when the wicked fall. Public life is shaped by private character.
The blessings of upright citizens lift a city up, but the words of the wicked tear it down.
Belittling your neighbor shows a lack of sense; a wise person knows when to stay quiet.

f.g: Keeps silent.

chapters.n: A gossip betrays confidences, but a trustworthy person keeps a secret.

f.g: talebearer = gossip, one who spreads rumors.

chapters.n: Without guidance a nation falls, but many advisers bring safety. Good decisions come from seeking counsel.

f.w: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety

chapters.n: Guaranteeing a stranger’s debt will hurt you; refusing such deals keeps you safe.

f.g: smart = suffer painfully.
suretiship = the practice of guaranteeing another’s debt.

chapters.n: A gracious woman gains honor, just as ruthless men gain wealth. The contrast suggests honor won by grace is better than riches seized by force.

f.g: Possibly “ruthless” or “violent men.”

chapters.n: Kindness benefits the kind person; cruelty hurts the one who is cruel.

f.w: The merciful man doeth good to his own soul

chapters.n: Wicked gains are deceptive and won’t last, but sowing righteousness brings a sure reward.
True righteousness leads to life; chasing evil leads to death.
The Lord detests the crooked in heart but delights in those whose ways are blameless.
Even if the wicked join forces, they won’t escape punishment; the righteous and their descendants will be rescued.

f.g: Possibly “be assured” (a pledge with the hand), or “even if they band together.”

chapters.n: A vivid, humorous image: a beautiful woman with no sense is like a gold ring in a pig’s nose—beauty wasted on what can’t honor it.

f.w: a jewel of gold in a swine's snout
f.g: Nose rings were common jewelry; pigs were unclean and rooted in the mud.
discretion = good sense, judgment.

chapters.n: The righteous desire only good; the hopes of the wicked end in wrath.

f.w: The desire of the righteous is only good

chapters.n: A paradox of generosity: some give freely and grow richer; others hoard and grow poorer.

f.g: meet = fitting, right.

chapters.n: A generous person will prosper; whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.

f.w: The liberal soul shall be made fat
f.g: liberal = generous; made fat = enriched, prospered.

f.w: he that watereth shall be watered also himself

chapters.n: People curse someone who hoards grain to raise prices in a shortage, but they bless the one who sells it fairly.

f.g: corn = grain (wheat or barley), not maize.

chapters.n: Whoever seeks good finds goodwill; whoever looks for trouble will find it.

f.g: procureth = obtains, gains.

chapters.n: Those who trust in riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like green leaves.

f.w: He that trusteth in his riches shall fall

f.g: Or “like a green leaf.”

chapters.n: Whoever brings trouble on their own family inherits only wind—nothing. The fool ends up serving the wise.

f.g: Gain nothing of substance.

chapters.n: The life of the righteous is like a tree of life, and the one who wins people’s hearts is wise. Latter-day Saints often apply the second line to sharing the gospel.

f.w: he that winneth souls is wise

chapters.n: If even the righteous face consequences in this life, how much more will the wicked. Peter quotes this verse (from the Greek version).

f.g: recompensed = repaid, given what is due.

f.w: much more the wicked and the sinner

chapters.n: Loving correction is the same as loving knowledge. Hating correction is acting like an animal without reason.

f.g: brutish = stupid, like a dumb animal.

chapters.n: The Lord shows favor to good people but condemns those who scheme.

f.g: devices = schemes, crafty plans.

chapters.n: Wickedness can’t give anyone a secure place, but the righteous are rooted firmly like a deep-rooted tree.

f.w: the root of the righteous shall not be moved

chapters.n: A woman of strong character brings honor to her husband like a crown; one who shames him is like a disease eating his bones.

f.g: Hebrew ʾeshet ḥayil—a woman of strength, worth, and capability.

chapters.n: The plans of the righteous are just; the advice of the wicked is deceptive.

f.g: counsels = advice, plans, strategies.

chapters.n: The words of the wicked set deadly ambushes, but the speech of the upright rescues people.
The wicked are overthrown and gone, but the house of the righteous stands firm.

f.w: the house of the righteous shall stand

chapters.n: People are praised for good sense; those with twisted minds are despised.

f.g: commended = praised.

chapters.n: Better to be an ordinary person who has a servant (that is, modest means) than to put on airs while having no food.

f.g: Plays the great man; pretends to be important.

chapters.n: Righteous people even care for the needs of their animals. Kindness reaches all creatures, while the wicked’s “kindness” is cruel.

f.w: regardeth the life of his beast

f.g: Their compassion—here, so-called compassion.

chapters.n: Working your land brings plenty of food, but chasing worthless pursuits shows a lack of sense.

f.g: vain = empty, worthless; or “worthless pursuits.”

chapters.n: The wicked covet what evil men catch, but the root of the righteous bears real fruit.

f.g: Possibly “the loot” or “stronghold” of evil men; the Hebrew is difficult.

chapters.n: Evil people are trapped by their own sinful talk, but the righteous escape trouble.

f.g: snared = caught in a trap.

chapters.n: Good words and good work both bring good returns. People reap what their mouths and hands produce.

f.w: the recompence of a man's hands
f.g: recompence = repayment, reward.

chapters.n: Fools think they are always right; wise people listen to advice.
A fool shows irritation immediately, but a sensible person overlooks an insult.

f.g: presently = immediately, at once.
Ignores an insult; doesn’t make a scene.

chapters.n: Telling the truth brings justice; a false witness spreads deceit.
Careless words can stab like a sword, but the words of the wise heal.

f.g: health = healing.

chapters.n: Truth lasts forever; a lie lasts only a moment.

f.w: The lip of truth shall be established for ever

chapters.n: Deceit fills the hearts of those who plot evil, but those who promote peace have joy.
A general principle: no lasting harm overtakes the righteous, while the wicked are full of trouble. Scripture elsewhere recognizes that the righteous still suffer in this life.

f.w: There shall no evil happen to the just

chapters.n: The Lord detests lying lips but delights in people who are trustworthy.

f.w: Lying lips are abomination to the LORD

chapters.n: A sensible person doesn’t show off what he knows, but fools broadcast their foolishness.

f.g: Holds back; doesn’t parade knowledge.

chapters.n: Diligent people end up leading; lazy people end up in forced labor.

f.g: Subject to forced labor or payments to others.
slothful = lazy.

chapters.n: Anxiety weighs a person down, but a kind word lifts them up. Encouragement is a real gift.

f.g: Weighs it down, depresses it.

f.w: a good word maketh it glad

chapters.n: The righteous are careful guides to their neighbors; the way of the wicked leads them astray.

f.w: is more excellent than his neighbour
f.g: Possibly “guides his neighbor” or “searches out his friends”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: A lazy hunter doesn’t even bother to cook what he caught; but diligence is a precious possession.

f.w: roasteth not that which he took in hunting

chapters.n: The road of righteousness leads to life—and on that path is no death. Some see here an early hint of immortality.
A wise child listens to a parent’s discipline; a scoffer refuses to listen to correction.
Good words bring good things back to the speaker, but treacherous people crave violence.
Guarding your words guards your life; speaking rashly brings ruin.

f.w: He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life

chapters.n: The lazy person wants things but gets nothing; the diligent are fully satisfied. Wishing is not the same as working.

f.g: Richly supplied, prosperous.

chapters.n: The righteous hate lies; the wicked act shamefully and bring disgrace.

f.g: Causing a stench—disgusting conduct.

chapters.n: Righteousness guards the person of integrity, but wickedness brings down the sinner.

f.g: keepeth = guards, protects.

chapters.n: Appearances deceive: some pretend to be rich but have nothing; others seem poor but have great wealth. Jesus warned about being rich in things but poor toward God.

f.w: maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches

chapters.n: A rich man may need to pay a ransom to save his life, but a poor man doesn’t even hear threats. Wealth can make you a target.

f.g: Doesn’t hear threats—no one bothers to threaten him.

chapters.n: The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out.

f.w: the lamp of the wicked shall be put out

chapters.n: Pride produces only quarrels; wisdom belongs to those who take advice.
Quick, dishonest wealth dwindles; wealth gathered little by little grows.

f.g: vanity = emptiness; here, quick or dishonest means.

f.w: he that gathereth by labour shall increase

chapters.n: Waiting endlessly for something you hope for can make the heart sick, but a fulfilled longing is like a tree of life. An honest picture of emotional experience.

f.w: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick
f.g: deferred = delayed, put off.

chapters.n: Whoever scorns instruction pays for it; whoever respects a command is rewarded.
The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life that helps a person escape death’s traps.
Good sense wins favor, but the way of the unfaithful is rough and leads to ruin.

f.w: the way of transgressors is hard
f.g: Or “is their ruin.”

chapters.n: Prudent people act with knowledge; fools put their foolishness on display.

f.g: Spreads it out like goods on a market stall.

chapters.n: An untrustworthy messenger causes trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.

f.g: An envoy, someone sent with a message.

chapters.n: Rejecting discipline leads to poverty and disgrace; accepting correction brings honor.

f.g: Takes correction seriously.

chapters.n: A fulfilled desire is sweet, but fools refuse to turn from evil even to get what they want.
Choose your friends carefully: you become like those you spend time with.

f.w: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise

chapters.n: Trouble chases sinners, while good things come to the righteous.
A good person leaves a legacy for grandchildren. Wealth gathered by sinners often ends up in the hands of the righteous.

f.w: an inheritance to his children's children

chapters.n: A poor person’s field can produce plenty of food, but injustice sweeps it away. The poor are often harmed by unfair systems, not just bad luck.

f.g: tillage = plowed land, fallow ground.
Lack of justice—injustice.

chapters.n: Loving parents discipline their children diligently; failing to correct a child is not kindness. The “rod” stood for discipline; modern readers should apply this with the love and gentleness the gospel teaches.

f.g: betimes = early, diligently, in good time.
chasteneth = disciplines, trains.

f.w: He that spareth his rod hateth his son

chapters.n: The righteous have enough to eat, but the wicked go hungry.

f.w: to the satisfying of his soul
f.g: Until his appetite is satisfied.

chapters.n: A wise woman builds up her household—her family and home—while a foolish one tears it down with her own hands. Homes are built or ruined by daily choices.
How we live shows what we think of God. An upright life shows reverence; a crooked life shows contempt.
A fool’s proud talk becomes a rod that strikes back at him; the words of the wise protect them.

f.g: Proud words that become a whip for his own back.

chapters.n: A practical farmer’s proverb: without oxen the stall stays clean, but you also get no big harvest. Productive work is messy, but worth it.

f.g: crib = feeding trough, manger.

chapters.n: An honest witness doesn’t lie; a false witness pours out lies.

f.w: A faithful witness will not lie

chapters.n: A mocker searches for wisdom and finds none, because his attitude blocks it. To the humble, knowledge comes easily.

f.w: A scorner seeketh wisdom, and findeth it not

chapters.n: Walk away from a fool when you notice his words have no knowledge in them.

f.w: Go from the presence of a foolish man

chapters.n: Wisdom helps a person understand where he is going; the folly of fools is self-deception.
Fools mock at making amends for sin, but among the upright there is goodwill.

f.w: Fools make a mock at sin
f.g: Possibly “fools mock the guilt offering”—they scorn making amends.

chapters.n: Each heart knows its own deepest sorrow and joy; no one else can fully share them. Only Christ fully understands our inner experience.

f.w: The heart knoweth his own bitterness

f.g: intermeddle = share in, take part in.

chapters.n: A wicked person’s solid house will fall, but even the tent of the upright will thrive.

f.g: tabernacle = tent, dwelling.

chapters.n: A sobering warning: a road can look right but end in death. Our own judgment needs God’s guidance. This saying repeats in 16:25.

f.w: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man

chapters.n: Laughter can hide a heavy heart, and joy may end in grief. Outward cheer doesn’t always reflect inner life.

f.g: heaviness = grief, sorrow.

chapters.n: The faithless will get their fill of their own ways, and good people will be rewarded for theirs.

f.g: backslider = one who turns away from the right path.

chapters.n: The naive believe anything they hear; prudent people think about where they are going.
The wise are cautious and steer clear of evil; fools are reckless and overconfident.

f.g: rageth = is reckless, careless, hot-headed.

chapters.n: A quick-tempered person acts foolishly, and a scheming person is hated.
The naive end up with folly as their inheritance; the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
In the end, evil people will bow before the good and beg at the gates of the righteous, as Joseph’s brothers bowed to him.

f.w: The evil bow before the good

chapters.n: A sad observation: the poor are shunned even by neighbors, while the rich have plenty of “friends.”
Looking down on a neighbor is sin; being kind to the needy brings happiness. Verse 20 describes; this verse commands.

f.w: he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he

chapters.n: Those who plot evil go astray, but those who plan good find love and faithfulness.

f.g: Steadfast love and faithfulness (ḥesed and ʾemet).

chapters.n: All hard work brings a profit, but mere talk leads only to poverty.

f.g: penury = poverty, want.

chapters.n: Wealth is a crown for the wise; folly is the only “crown” fools receive.
A truthful witness can save lives in court; a false one only deceives.

f.g: Saves lives—in a trial, honest testimony can save an innocent person.

chapters.n: Reverence for the Lord gives a secure fortress, and his children will have refuge.
Reverence for the Lord is a life-giving spring that helps one avoid death’s traps. Compare 13:14, where the same is said of wise teaching.
A king’s glory is in having many people; a ruler without subjects is ruined. Leaders are only as strong as the people they serve.
Patience shows great understanding; a hot temper shows off foolishness.

f.w: He that is slow to wrath

chapters.n: A peaceful heart gives life to the body, but envy rots the bones. Our inner state affects our physical health.

f.g: A calm, tranquil, healthy heart.

f.w: envy the rottenness of the bones

chapters.n: Oppressing the poor insults their Creator, because they are made in his image. Kindness to the needy honors God.
The wicked are brought down by their own evil, but the righteous find refuge even in death.

f.w: the righteous hath hope in his death

chapters.n: Wisdom rests quietly in a discerning heart; even among fools it makes itself known.

f.g: Settles in, makes itself at home.

chapters.n: Righteousness lifts a nation up; sin brings disgrace on any people. The Book of Mormon shows this pattern again and again.

f.g: reproach = disgrace.

chapters.n: A king favors a wise servant but is angry with one who acts shamefully.
A gentle reply can calm someone’s anger; harsh words fan the flames. One of the most practical verses in Proverbs for family life and friendships.

f.w: A soft answer turneth away wrath

f.g: Hurtful, harsh words.

chapters.n: The wise use knowledge well when they speak; fools gush out foolishness.

f.g: Gushes, bubbles over like a spring.

chapters.n: God sees everywhere and watches both evil and good people. Nothing is hidden from him.

f.w: The eyes of the LORD are in every place

chapters.n: Healing words are like a tree of life; twisted words crush the spirit.

f.g: A healing, soothing tongue.
A wound or break in the spirit.

chapters.n: A fool rejects a parent’s discipline; whoever accepts correction shows good sense.

f.g: prudent = sensible, shrewd in a good way.

chapters.n: The home of the righteous holds real treasure; the earnings of the wicked bring trouble.

f.g: revenues = income, earnings.

chapters.n: Wise people spread knowledge like a farmer scattering seed; the hearts of fools are not like that.

f.g: disperse = scatter, spread abroad, like seed.

chapters.n: God detests sacrifices offered by wicked people—worship without a changed life is empty. But the prayer of the upright delights him.

f.w: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination
the prayer of the upright is his delight

chapters.n: God detests the way of the wicked but loves those who pursue righteousness.
Discipline feels harsh to someone who has left the right path; refusing correction leads to death.

f.g: grievous = painful, severe.

chapters.n: If even the underworld and the realm of destruction lie open before God, how much more can he see human hearts.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol and Abaddon—the grave and the place of destruction.

f.w: the hearts of the children of men

chapters.n: A mocker resents being corrected and avoids the wise.

f.w: neither will he go unto the wise

chapters.n: A happy heart shows on the face; heartache crushes the spirit. Inner life shapes outward appearance.

f.g: countenance = face, expression.

chapters.n: A discerning heart hungers for knowledge; a fool’s mouth feeds on foolishness. We become what we consume.
For the miserable every day is hard, but a cheerful heart enjoys a continual feast. Attitude changes how life is experienced.
Better to have little and revere the Lord than great wealth with turmoil.
A simple meal of vegetables with love is better than a feast of fattened beef with hatred. Relationships matter more than luxuries.

f.g: A plain vegetable meal—a poor person’s food.
A fattened ox kept in a stall—the finest meat.

chapters.n: A hot-tempered person stirs up conflict; a patient one calms a quarrel.

f.g: Calms a dispute.

chapters.n: The lazy person’s path seems blocked by thorns—everything is an obstacle. The path of the upright is a smooth highway.
A wise child brings joy to a father; a foolish one shows contempt for a mother.

f.w: A wise son maketh a glad father

chapters.n: Folly brings joy to someone lacking sense, but a person of understanding keeps a straight course.

f.g: Literally “lacking heart.”

chapters.n: Plans fail without advice but succeed with many advisers.
It is a joy to give a fitting answer, and how good is a word at just the right time!

f.w: a word spoken in due season

chapters.n: The path of life leads upward for the wise, away from the grave below.

f.g: Sheol below—the grave, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: The Lord tears down the house of the proud but protects the widow’s property lines. God defends the vulnerable.

f.g: Her boundary stones—powerful people sometimes moved them to steal land.

chapters.n: God detests evil thoughts, but gracious words are pure to him.
Greed for dishonest gain brings trouble on one’s household; whoever hates bribes will live.

f.g: Here, bribes.

chapters.n: A righteous person thinks before answering; the wicked blurt out evil.

f.g: Thinks carefully how to answer.

chapters.n: The Lord is far from the wicked but hears the prayers of the righteous.

f.w: he heareth the prayer of the righteous

chapters.n: A bright face cheers the heart, and good news refreshes the body.

f.g: Good news.
Refreshes and strengthens the body.

chapters.n: Whoever listens to life-giving correction will be at home among the wise.

f.g: Correction that leads to life.

chapters.n: Rejecting discipline is self-harm; accepting correction brings understanding.
Reverence for the Lord is the school of wisdom, and humility comes before honor. Jesus taught that the humble will be exalted.
People make plans in their hearts, but the final word belongs to the Lord. Several verses in this chapter explore how human planning and God’s guidance work together.

f.g: The plans or arrangements of the mind.

chapters.n: We tend to think all our actions are fine, but the Lord weighs our motives. He sees what lies beneath the surface.
Entrust your work to the Lord, and your plans will succeed. Literally, “roll” your works onto him.

f.g: Literally “roll”—roll your burden onto the Lord.

chapters.n: The Lord has a purpose for everything, and even the wicked will meet their day of judgment. This doesn’t mean God makes people wicked; it means no one escapes his justice.

f.g: Or “for its purpose / its answer.”
The day of calamity or judgment.

chapters.n: The Lord detests the proud; be sure of it, they will not go unpunished.

f.g: Possibly “be assured” (a pledge by handshake).

chapters.n: Steadfast love and faithfulness atone for sin, and reverence for the Lord leads people away from evil. Latter-day Saints see ultimate atonement in Christ, whose mercy and truth meet.

f.g: purged = atoned for, covered.

chapters.n: When a person’s ways please God, he can make even enemies live at peace with them—as with Jacob and Esau.

f.w: his enemies to be at peace with him

chapters.n: Better a little gained honestly than great income gained unjustly.

f.w: Better is a little with righteousness

chapters.n: We plan our route, but the Lord guides our steps. Make plans—but stay open to his direction.
An ideal: a king speaks with God-given authority and should not betray justice. Verses 10–15 describe what a righteous king should be.

f.g: An inspired decision, almost like an oracle.

chapters.n: Honest scales and weights belong to the Lord. Fair business is his concern too.

f.w: all the weights of the bag
f.g: Merchants carried stone weights in a pouch for weighing silver.

chapters.n: Kings should detest wrongdoing, because a throne stands firm on righteousness.

f.w: the throne is established by righteousness

chapters.n: Good rulers value honest advisers and those who speak the truth.
A king’s anger can mean death, but a wise person will calm it.

f.g: pacify = calm, appease.

chapters.n: The king’s favor is life-giving, like the spring rain clouds that ripen the harvest.

f.w: a cloud of the latter rain
f.g: The spring rains (March–April) that matured crops before harvest.

chapters.n: Getting wisdom is far better than getting gold, and understanding is better than silver.

f.w: How much better is it to get wisdom than gold

chapters.n: The highway of the upright avoids evil; whoever watches his path guards his life.

f.g: A raised, cleared road—a straight, well-made path.

chapters.n: Perhaps the best-known proverb: pride comes before disaster and arrogance before a fall. The Book of Mormon’s “pride cycle” illustrates it repeatedly.

f.g: haughty = arrogant, lofty.

chapters.n: Better to be humble among the poor than to share loot with the proud.

f.g: Share the plunder after battle.

chapters.n: Paying attention to instruction brings good results, and trusting the Lord brings true happiness.

f.w: whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he

chapters.n: The wise are recognized as discerning, and pleasant speech makes teaching more persuasive.

f.w: the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning
f.g: Gracious speech makes instruction more persuasive.

chapters.n: Understanding is a fountain of life to its owner; fools are disciplined by their own folly.

f.g: wellspring = a fountain, source of water.

chapters.n: A wise heart guides the mouth and makes speech persuasive.

f.w: The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth

chapters.n: Kind words are like honey—sweet to the soul and healing to the body.

f.g: Healing for the whole body.

chapters.n: This repeats 14:12 word for word: a path can seem right yet lead to death. The repetition emphasizes how easily we deceive ourselves.

f.w: There is a way that seemeth right unto a man

chapters.n: Hunger motivates a worker; his appetite drives him on. Need can be a healthy spur to labor.

f.w: his mouth craveth it of him
f.g: His hunger urges him on.

chapters.n: A worthless person digs up trouble like someone digging a pit, and his words burn like fire.

f.g: Hebrew “man of belial”—a worthless scoundrel.

chapters.n: A perverse person spreads conflict, and a gossip separates close friends.

f.g: whisperer = gossip, slanderer.
Close, intimate friends.

chapters.n: A violent person lures a neighbor into wrongdoing. Evil often recruits.
Squinting eyes and pursed lips—body language of someone plotting harm.

f.g: Winks or narrows his eyes, a sign of scheming.

chapters.n: Gray hair is a crown of glory when it comes through a righteous life. Old age lived well is honorable.

f.g: hoary = gray or white with age.

chapters.n: Self-control is greater than military might. Ruling your own temper is harder than conquering a city.
Lots—like dice—were thrown into a fold of the garment to make decisions, but the outcome is in God’s hands. Nothing is mere chance to him.

f.w: The lot is cast into the lap
f.g: Casting lots was a common way of making decisions in Israel.

chapters.n: Better a dry crust eaten in peace than a house full of feasting with conflict. Sacrificial meat was often eaten at feasts, so this means a house full of party food.

f.g: A crust of bread with no oil or dip.
Feasts—meat from peace offerings was eaten at celebrations.

chapters.n: A wise servant can rise above a shameful son and even share the family inheritance. Character can count for more than birth.

f.w: A wise servant shall have rule

chapters.n: Silver and gold are refined by intense heat, but the Lord tests hearts. Trials can purify us.

f.g: fining pot = a crucible for refining metal.

chapters.n: Wrongdoers eagerly listen to wicked talk, and liars give ear to destructive words. People seek out what matches their character.

f.g: A destructive, wicked tongue.

chapters.n: Mocking the poor insults their Creator; delighting in someone else’s disaster won’t go unpunished.
Grandchildren are the crown of the elderly, and parents are the pride of their children. Families bless each other across generations.

f.w: Children's children are the crown of old men

chapters.n: Fine speech doesn’t suit a fool, and lying suits a leader even less.

f.g: becometh = suits, is fitting for.

chapters.n: To the one who gives it, a bribe seems like a magic stone that opens every door. This describes how people view bribes; other verses condemn them.

f.g: Here, a bribe.

chapters.n: Overlooking an offense builds love; repeating it spreads division and breaks up close friends.

f.w: He that covereth a transgression seeketh love

f.g: Close friends.

chapters.n: One rebuke goes deeper into a wise person than a hundred lashes into a fool.

f.g: stripes = lashes, blows.

chapters.n: A rebel seeks only trouble, so a stern messenger will be sent against him.

f.g: A merciless messenger—perhaps an executioner or messenger of judgment.

chapters.n: Humorous and vivid: you’d be safer meeting an enraged mother bear than a fool caught up in his folly.

f.w: a bear robbed of her whelps
f.g: whelps = cubs.

chapters.n: Whoever repays good with evil will find evil never leaves his household—as David learned after his sin against Uriah.
Starting a quarrel is like opening a floodgate—once the water flows, it’s hard to stop. Drop the matter before it breaks out.

f.g: Like a small crack in a dam that quickly becomes a flood.

chapters.n: Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent are both detestable to God. Justice must be fair both ways.
What good is money in a fool’s hand to buy wisdom when he has no desire for it? Wisdom can’t be bought without a willing heart.

f.w: he hath no heart to it
f.g: He has no sense or desire to learn.

chapters.n: A true friend loves through every season, and family members are born to help in hard times.

f.w: A friend loveth at all times

f.g: adversity = hardship, distress.

chapters.n: Only a person lacking sense shakes hands to co-sign a neighbor’s debt.

f.g: Shakes hands to seal a pledge.

chapters.n: Loving conflict means loving sin. Building a high gate—showing off—invites disaster.

f.g: Builds a lofty doorway—a show of pride; or “opens his mouth wide” in boasting.

chapters.n: A crooked heart finds no good, and a deceitful tongue lands in trouble.

f.g: froward = crooked, perverse.

chapters.n: Raising a fool brings grief; the father of a godless fool has no joy.

f.g: Here Hebrew naval—a morally empty, godless person.

chapters.n: A cheerful heart is good medicine; a crushed spirit dries a person up. Joy has real effects on health.

f.w: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine

chapters.n: A wicked person secretly accepts a bribe from under the cloak to twist justice.

f.g: From a fold in the garment—slipped secretly.

chapters.n: The discerning keep wisdom in view; a fool’s eyes wander to the ends of the earth, never focused.

f.w: the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth
f.g: His attention drifts everywhere except what matters.

chapters.n: A foolish child brings grief to a father and bitterness to a mother.

f.g: His mother—she who bore him.

chapters.n: It is wrong to punish the innocent or to strike noble people for doing what is right.

f.g: equity = uprightness, fairness.

chapters.n: A person of knowledge uses words with restraint and keeps a calm, cool spirit.

f.g: Literally “cool of spirit”—calm, even-tempered.

chapters.n: Even a fool seems wise if he keeps quiet. Silence is sometimes the wisest speech.

A hard verse. The KJV reads it as praise for one who withdraws to seek wisdom. Many modern translations read it the other way: a person who isolates himself pursues his own desires and rejects sound judgment.

f.g: The Hebrew is debated: either withdrawing to study, or selfishly cutting himself off from others.
intermeddleth = engages with, or quarrels against.

chapters.n: A fool doesn’t care to understand; he only wants to air his own opinions.

f.w: that his heart may discover itself
f.g: discover = reveal, uncover—to show off his own views.

chapters.n: Wickedness brings contempt with it, and shameful behavior brings disgrace.

f.g: ignominy = dishonor, public shame.

chapters.n: A person’s words can run deep like waters; the source of wisdom flows like a fresh, bubbling brook.
It is wrong to show favor to the guilty or to deny justice to the innocent.

f.w: accept the person of the wicked
f.g: Show partiality—literally “lift up the face” of the wicked.

chapters.n: A fool’s words start fights, and his mouth practically invites a beating.

f.g: strokes = blows, beatings.

chapters.n: A fool’s own mouth ruins him; his words become a trap for his life.
Gossip is like tasty bites of food that people swallow eagerly—and it sinks deep inside. The image is about how easily rumors are absorbed.

f.g: Hebrew likely means “delicious morsels”—gossip is tempting to swallow.

chapters.n: Laziness is a close relative of destruction. Neglect destroys as surely as wastefulness.

f.g: A destroyer; one who ruins things.

chapters.n: The Lord’s name—his character and presence—is a tall fortress where the righteous run and find safety.

f.w: The name of the LORD is a strong tower

chapters.n: The rich imagine their wealth is a fortress and a high wall around them—but it’s only in their imagination. Compare verse 10.

f.g: In his own imagination.
