chapters.n: Pride comes right before destruction, and humility comes before honor.
Answering before you’ve heard the whole story is foolish and embarrassing. Listen first.

f.w: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it

chapters.n: A person’s spirit can carry them through physical illness, but who can endure a crushed spirit? Emotional wounds are among the heaviest.

f.g: infirmity = sickness, weakness.

f.w: a wounded spirit who can bear?

chapters.n: Discerning hearts acquire knowledge, and wise ears go looking for it.
A gift opens doors and gains access to important people. This observes how influence works; it can be used well or badly.
The first to tell his side in a dispute sounds right—until someone else cross-examines him. Hear both sides.

f.g: Examines, questions him closely.

chapters.n: Casting lots settled disputes and kept powerful rivals from fighting.

f.g: Lots were cast to decide matters, trusting God to direct the result.

chapters.n: A wounded brother is harder to win back than a fortified city; family quarrels are like locked castle gates.

f.g: Heavy bolts on a fortress gate.

chapters.n: Your words are like crops: you’ll eat the harvest of what you say.
The tongue holds the power of life and death; those who love to talk will eat the results.

f.w: Death and life are in the power of the tongue

chapters.n: Finding a wife is finding something good, a sign of the Lord’s favor. Marriage is seen as a blessing from God.

f.w: Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing

chapters.n: The poor must plead for mercy, while the rich answer harshly. An honest observation about how wealth can change people.

f.g: entreaties = earnest pleas for mercy.

chapters.n: The KJV says to have friends, be friendly. Many translators read: a person of many companions may come to ruin, but a true friend sticks closer than a brother. Christians often see the Savior as that truest friend.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean “may come to ruin”—too many shallow friends can harm you.

f.w: a friend that sticketh closer than a brother

chapters.n: Better to be poor and honest than to be a smooth-talking fool. Integrity outweighs wealth.
Zeal without knowledge isn’t good, and rushing ahead makes you miss the way.

f.w: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth
f.g: sinneth = misses the mark, loses the way.

chapters.n: People ruin their lives through their own foolishness—and then blame and rage against the Lord.

f.w: his heart fretteth against the LORD
f.g: fretteth = rages, is angry.

chapters.n: Money attracts many friends, but the poor are deserted even by their neighbor.
A false witness will be punished, and a liar won’t get away with it.

f.w: A false witness shall not be unpunished

chapters.n: Many seek favor from a ruler, and everyone is a friend to the person who gives gifts.

f.g: Literally “stroke the face”—flatter, curry favor.

chapters.n: The poor are shunned even by relatives, and friends keep their distance. He chases after them with pleas, but they are gone.

f.g: They are not there for him—nowhere to be found.

chapters.n: Getting wisdom is loving yourself rightly; keeping understanding leads to good.

f.g: Truly cares for his own life and well-being.

chapters.n: Repeats verse 5, but with a sharper ending: the liar will perish.
Luxury doesn’t suit a fool, and it’s even worse for a slave to rule over princes—things out of their proper order.

f.g: seemly = fitting, appropriate.

f.w: a servant to have rule over princes

chapters.n: Good sense makes a person patient, and it is to their credit to overlook an offense.

f.g: deferreth = delays, holds back.

chapters.n: A king’s anger is terrifying like a lion’s roar, but his favor is refreshing like dew on grass.
A foolish son brings ruin to his father, and a quarrelsome wife is like a constant leaky roof.

f.g: A steady drip from a leaky roof during a rainstorm.

chapters.n: Houses and wealth can be inherited from parents, but a wise spouse is a gift from the Lord.

f.w: a prudent wife is from the LORD

chapters.n: Laziness brings on deep sleep, and the idle go hungry.

f.g: slothfulness = laziness.

chapters.n: Keeping the commandments protects your life; carelessness about your conduct leads to death.
Being kind to the poor is like lending to the Lord himself, and he will repay. King Benjamin taught the same principle.
Discipline your child while there is still hope; don’t let them destroy themselves. Many translations read the second line, “don’t set your heart on his death.”

f.w: let not thy soul spare for his crying
f.g: Or “do not set your heart on putting him to death”—don’t let neglect lead to his ruin.

chapters.n: A hot-tempered person must pay the consequences; if you rescue him, you’ll have to do it again and again.

f.g: Bailing someone out repeatedly doesn’t change them.

chapters.n: Listen to advice and accept instruction so you will be wise in the end.

f.g: Later in life, or in the end.

chapters.n: People make many plans, but the Lord’s purpose is what prevails.

f.w: the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand

chapters.n: What people really want is loyal love; better to be poor than a liar.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed—loyal, faithful love.

chapters.n: Reverence for the Lord leads to life; such a person rests content and untouched by harm.

f.w: The fear of the LORD tendeth to life

chapters.n: A comic picture: the sluggard dips his hand in the dish but is too lazy to lift it back to his mouth.

f.w: hideth his hand in his bosom
f.g: Better “buries his hand in the dish”—the shared bowl of food.

chapters.n: Punish a mocker and the naive will learn a lesson; correct a discerning person and they’ll gain knowledge.

f.w: Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware

chapters.n: A child who robs his father and drives out his mother brings shame and disgrace.

f.g: Ruins or robs his father.

chapters.n: Stop listening to teaching that leads you away from true knowledge.

f.w: the instruction that causeth to err

chapters.n: A corrupt witness mocks justice, and the wicked gulp down evil like food.

f.g: A “witness of belial”—a worthless, corrupt witness.

chapters.n: Penalties are prepared for mockers and beatings for fools.

f.g: stripes = lashes.

chapters.n: Wine and strong drink are pictured as people: one mocks, the other brawls. Anyone led astray by them is not wise. Latter-day Saints see this principle carried further in the Word of Wisdom.

f.g: Beer or other fermented drink.

chapters.n: A king’s fury is like a lion’s roar; whoever provokes him risks his own life.

f.g: The terror a king inspires; his wrath.

chapters.n: It is honorable to avoid a fight; only fools are quick to quarrel.

f.g: Quick to break out in a quarrel.

chapters.n: The lazy farmer won’t plow in the chilly autumn, so at harvest he looks for a crop and finds nothing.

f.g: Plowing happened in autumn, at the start of the rainy season.

chapters.n: A person’s real purposes lie deep like water in a well, but a discerning person can draw them out—a good description of a wise counselor or listener.

f.g: Like drawing water up from a deep well.

chapters.n: Many people claim to be loyal and good, but a truly faithful person is hard to find.

f.w: a faithful man who can find?

chapters.n: The righteous live with integrity, and their children are blessed after them. Good character becomes a family legacy.

f.w: his children are blessed after him

chapters.n: A king on his judgment seat sees through evil and scatters it, the way a farmer winnows chaff.

f.g: Winnows—separating grain from chaff.

chapters.n: Who can honestly claim to have a perfectly clean heart, free from sin? No one—everyone needs God’s mercy.

f.w: I am pure from my sin

chapters.n: Using two sets of weights and measures—one for buying, one for selling—is detestable to the Lord.

f.g: divers = different, varying; a heavy weight for buying and a light one for selling.

chapters.n: Even children show their character by what they do—whether their conduct is pure and right.

f.w: Even a child is known by his doings

chapters.n: Ears that hear and eyes that see were both made by the Lord. He gave us these senses, and he himself sees and hears all.

f.w: The hearing ear, and the seeing eye

chapters.n: Don’t love sleep or you will grow poor; stay awake and you’ll have plenty of food.
A slice of market life: the buyer complains “It’s no good!” while haggling—then brags about his bargain afterward.

f.g: naught = worthless, bad.

chapters.n: Gold and jewels are plentiful, but lips that speak knowledge are a rare treasure.
If someone foolishly guarantees a stranger’s debt, take his coat as collateral. He has shown he is a risk.

f.g: A cloak was taken as a pledge (collateral) for a loan.

chapters.n: Food gained by deceit tastes sweet at first, but later it’s like a mouthful of gravel.
Make plans by seeking advice; if you wage war, get guidance first.
A gossip betrays confidences, so avoid anyone who talks too much.

f.g: talebearer = gossip, slanderer.

f.w: him that flattereth with his lips
f.g: Or “one who opens his lips wide”—a chatterer.

chapters.n: Whoever curses father or mother will have his lamp snuffed out in deep darkness. Under the law of Moses this was a capital offense.

f.w: Whoso curseth his father or his mother

f.g: Pitch-black darkness, like the middle of the night.

chapters.n: An inheritance grabbed too quickly at the beginning won’t be blessed in the end—like the prodigal son who demanded his share early.
Don’t say, “I’ll get even.” Wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you.
The Lord detests dishonest weights; rigged scales are not good. (Compare verse 10.)

f.w: a false balance is not good

chapters.n: The Lord directs a person’s steps; how then can anyone fully understand his own path? We see only part of the road.

f.w: Man's goings are of the LORD

chapters.n: It’s a trap to rashly dedicate something to God and only think it over later. Make vows carefully.

f.g: Rashly declares something holy, dedicating it to God.

chapters.n: A wise king sifts out the wicked like a farmer threshing grain by driving a wheel over it.

f.g: A threshing wheel or cart was rolled over grain to separate it from the husk.

chapters.n: The human spirit is like the Lord’s lamp, searching out a person’s innermost being. Latter-day Saints may think of the light of Christ given to everyone.

f.w: The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD

f.g: candle = lamp (an olive-oil lamp).

chapters.n: Loyal love and faithfulness protect a king; his throne is secured through love.

f.w: Mercy and truth preserve the king

chapters.n: Each age has its glory: young people have strength, and the old have the dignity of gray hair.
Blows that wound can scrub away evil; punishment can reach deep inside. Correction, though painful, can bring real change.

f.g: Bruises from a beating.

f.w: the inward parts of the belly
f.g: The innermost being.

chapters.n: Even a powerful king’s heart is in God’s hand, as easily directed as a farmer channels irrigation water. No ruler is beyond God’s reach.

f.g: Irrigation channels that a farmer opens or closes to guide water.

chapters.n: People think their ways are right, but the Lord weighs hearts. (Compare 16:2.)

f.g: pondereth = weighs.

chapters.n: Doing what is right and just pleases the Lord more than sacrifice. Ritual cannot replace righteous living—a theme the prophets repeat.

f.w: more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice

chapters.n: Haughty eyes and a proud heart—the very “lamp” that guides the wicked—are sin.

f.g: Hebrew can be read “the lamp of the wicked”—what guides their life.

chapters.n: Careful planning by diligent people leads to profit; hasty shortcuts lead to poverty.

f.g: plenteousness = abundance.

chapters.n: A fortune made by lying is a vanishing mist and a deadly trap.

f.w: a vanity tossed to and fro
f.g: A fleeting vapor blown away.

chapters.n: The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is right.

f.g: Literally “drag them away,” as in a net.

chapters.n: The path of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the innocent is upright.

f.g: Crooked and devious.

chapters.n: Better to live in a cramped corner of the roof than share a big house with a quarrelsome spouse. Flat roofs in Israel could hold a small room or shelter.

f.g: Flat roofs were living space; a corner offered little room or shelter.
brawling = quarrelsome, nagging.

chapters.n: The wicked crave evil; they show no mercy even to their neighbors.

f.w: findeth no favour in his eyes
f.g: Receives no compassion from him.

chapters.n: When a mocker is punished, the naive learn; when the wise are taught, they grow in knowledge.
The Righteous One—likely God—observes the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin.

f.g: Possibly “the Righteous One,” a title for God.

chapters.n: Whoever ignores the cries of the poor will one day cry out and not be answered.

f.w: Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor

chapters.n: A secret gift calms anger, and a bribe hidden in a cloak soothes fury. An observation of how things work, not an endorsement of bribery.

f.g: A gift slipped secretly into the fold of a garment.

chapters.n: Justice brings joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.

f.w: It is joy to the just to do judgment

chapters.n: Whoever strays from the path of wisdom ends up resting among the dead.

f.g: The assembly of the rephaim—the shades of the dead.

chapters.n: Whoever loves pleasure and luxury (wine and perfumed oil) will end up poor.

f.g: Symbols of feasting and luxury.

chapters.n: The wicked become the ransom for the righteous: trouble meant for the good falls on the wicked instead.
Better to live alone in the desert than with a contentious, angry spouse.

f.g: contentious = quarrelsome, argumentative.

chapters.n: The wise have precious stores and oil in their homes, but fools gulp down all they have.

f.g: Swallows it all, uses it up.

chapters.n: Whoever pursues righteousness and loyal love finds life, righteousness, and honor.
Wisdom is stronger than military power: a wise person can capture a city of warriors and tear down the stronghold they trusted.

f.w: scaleth the city of the mighty

chapters.n: Guarding your mouth and tongue keeps you out of trouble.
The proud and arrogant person’s name is “Mocker”—he acts with insolent pride.

f.g: scorner = mocker, scoffer.

chapters.n: The lazy person’s cravings will kill him, because his hands refuse to work.

f.w: The desire of the slothful killeth him

chapters.n: The lazy covet all day long, but the righteous give without holding back.

f.w: the righteous giveth and spareth not

chapters.n: God detests the sacrifice of the wicked—even more when it’s offered with evil intent, like buying off God.

f.w: The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination

chapters.n: A false witness will be destroyed, but a person who listens carefully will speak with lasting credibility.

f.g: Speaks lastingly—his testimony stands.

chapters.n: The wicked put up a bold, brazen front, but the upright think carefully about their path.

f.g: Shows a bold, shameless face.

chapters.n: No human wisdom, insight, or plan can succeed against the Lord.

f.w: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD

chapters.n: You can prepare horses for battle, but victory comes from the Lord. Prepare diligently—then trust God for the outcome.

f.g: Or “victory belongs to the Lord.”

chapters.n: A good reputation is worth more than great wealth, and being well thought of is better than silver or gold.

f.g: Esteem, goodwill from others.

chapters.n: Rich and poor share one thing: the Lord made them both. Every person has equal worth before God.

f.w: the LORD is the maker of them all

chapters.n: The prudent see danger coming and take cover; the naive keep going and pay for it.

f.w: A prudent man foreseeth the evil

chapters.n: Humility and reverence for the Lord bring riches, honor, and life.
Thorns and traps line the road of the crooked; those who guard their lives stay far away.

A beloved promise to parents: teach a child well and that training tends to last a lifetime. It is a general principle, not a guarantee—children have agency—but early teaching has deep, lasting influence.

f.g: Train = dedicate, start off; possibly “according to his way,” suited to the child.

f.w: when he is old, he will not depart from it

chapters.n: An honest observation about money: the rich rule over the poor, and borrowers become servants to lenders. A strong caution against debt.

f.w: the borrower is servant to the lender

chapters.n: Whoever sows injustice will reap disaster, and the rod he used in anger will be broken.

f.w: He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity

chapters.n: A generous person will be blessed because he shares his food with the poor.

f.g: Literally “a good eye”—a generous, kindly outlook.

chapters.n: Remove the mocker and quarrels leave with him; strife and insults stop.
Whoever loves a pure heart and speaks graciously will have the king as a friend.
The Lord watches over true knowledge but frustrates the words of the treacherous.

f.w: The eyes of the LORD preserve knowledge

chapters.n: A humorous excuse: the lazy person won’t go out to work because “there’s a lion outside!” Any excuse will do.

f.g: without = outside.

chapters.n: The adulteress’s mouth is a deep pit, and those under God’s displeasure fall into it.

f.g: abhorred = regarded with disgust; under God’s wrath.

chapters.n: Children naturally have foolishness bound up in them, and loving discipline helps drive it away. The “rod” stands for correction; the gospel calls for discipline given with love and gentleness.
Oppressing the poor to get rich, or giving gifts to the rich to win favor, both lead to poverty.

A new collection, “the words of the wise,” begins here and runs to 24:22. Many scholars note similarities between it and an Egyptian wisdom text, the Instruction of Amenemope. It opens with a call to listen.

f.g: A heading for a new section of the book (22:17–24:22).

chapters.n: It’s good to keep these sayings in your heart and have them ready on your lips.

f.g: withal = together, at the same time.

chapters.n: The purpose of these teachings: that your trust will be in the Lord. Wisdom is ultimately about faith.

f.w: That thy trust may be in the LORD

chapters.n: The teacher asks: haven’t I written for you excellent sayings of counsel and knowledge? Some translate “thirty sayings,” matching Amenemope’s thirty chapters.

f.g: The Hebrew may read “thirty sayings,” a possible structural note for this section.

chapters.n: These teachings give you confidence in what is true, so you can bring back reliable answers to those who sent you.

f.w: the certainty of the words of truth

chapters.n: Don’t exploit the poor because they are weak, or crush the needy in court. The gate was where legal cases were judged.

f.g: The city gate, where elders heard legal cases.

chapters.n: The Lord himself will take up the case of the poor and will plunder those who plundered them.

f.w: the LORD will plead their cause

f.g: spoil = plunder, rob.

chapters.n: Don’t make friends with a hot-tempered person or spend time with someone easily angered.

f.w: Make no friendship with an angry man

chapters.n: You might pick up his habits and get yourself trapped.
Don’t be one who shakes hands to guarantee other people’s debts.

f.g: Shake hands to seal a pledge.

chapters.n: If you can’t pay, even your bed may be taken from under you. Co-signing puts your basic necessities at risk.
Don’t move the ancient boundary stones your ancestors set. Moving them was a sneaky way to steal land.

f.g: Boundary stones marking a family’s inherited land.

chapters.n: Do you see someone skilled at their work? They will serve kings, not obscure people. Excellence opens doors—as with Joseph and Daniel.

f.g: Skilled, quick, competent.
mean = obscure, lowly, unimportant.

chapters.n: Advice for dining with a powerful person: be careful and pay attention to what (or who) is in front of you.

f.w: consider diligently what is before thee
f.g: Or “who is before you”—be aware of the ruler’s motives.

chapters.n: A vivid way to say “control your appetite”: put a knife to your throat if you tend to overindulge.

f.g: Greedy, inclined to overeat.

chapters.n: Don’t crave the ruler’s delicacies, because that food may be a trap—offered to win influence over you.

f.g: dainties = delicacies, fancy food.

chapters.n: Don’t wear yourself out to get rich; have the good sense to stop.
Riches vanish in a blink—they sprout wings and fly off like an eagle. Strikingly, an Egyptian wisdom text uses a similar image of riches flying away like geese.
Don’t eat with a stingy person or crave his fancy food.

f.g: A stingy, grudging attitude (the opposite of the “bountiful eye” of 22:9).

chapters.n: He’s always counting the cost. He says “eat and drink,” but he doesn’t mean it. A person’s true character is what is in his heart.

f.w: as he thinketh in his heart, so is he
f.g: In context: he is the kind of man who calculates in his heart.

chapters.n: You’ll regret the bite you ate and waste your polite compliments on him.

f.g: Your pleasant words will have been wasted.

chapters.n: Don’t waste wise words on fools; they’ll only scorn them.

f.w: Speak not in the ears of a fool

chapters.n: Don’t move old boundary stones or steal the fields of orphans.

f.g: Orphans, among the most vulnerable in ancient society.

chapters.n: Their Redeemer is strong and will take up their case against you. A “redeemer” (go’el) was a close relative who defended family rights; here God himself is the defender. Latter-day Saints see in this title the Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

f.g: Hebrew go’el—a kinsman-protector who rescued family members and land.

chapters.n: Commit your heart to discipline and your ears to knowledge.
Don’t hold back correction from a child; discipline won’t kill him. The ancient world used physical punishment; the lasting principle is that loving correction protects a child.

f.w: Withhold not correction from the child

chapters.n: Correction can save a child from ruin and early death. The parent’s goal is the child’s life, not punishment for its own sake.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, death.

chapters.n: A parent speaks with emotion: if your heart is wise, my heart will be glad too.
My innermost being will rejoice when you speak what is right.

f.g: reins = kidneys; in Hebrew thought, the seat of the deepest emotions.

chapters.n: Don’t envy sinners; keep reverencing the Lord all day long.

f.w: Let not thine heart envy sinners

chapters.n: There truly is a future, and your hope will not be cut off. The righteous can trust that things will be set right.

f.w: thine expectation shall not be cut off

chapters.n: Listen, my child, be wise, and keep your heart on the right path.

f.w: guide thine heart in the way

chapters.n: Don’t join heavy drinkers or those who gorge on meat.

f.g: winebibbers = heavy drinkers.
Gluttons who gorge themselves on meat.

chapters.n: Drunkards and gluttons end up poor, and their drowsiness leaves them in rags.

f.w: drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags

chapters.n: Listen to the father who gave you life, and don’t look down on your mother when she is old. Honoring parents continues through their old age.

f.w: despise not thy mother when she is old

chapters.n: Buy truth and never sell it—along with wisdom, instruction, and understanding. Truth is worth any price and shouldn’t be traded away.

f.w: Buy the truth, and sell it not

chapters.n: The father of a righteous child greatly rejoices; a wise child brings joy.
Let your father and mother be glad—give her who bore you reason to rejoice.

f.g: Your mother, who gave birth to you.

chapters.n: The father pleads, “Give me your heart,” and watch my example. Real teaching is about trust and example, not just rules.
A prostitute is like a deep ditch, and an adulteress a narrow well—easy to fall into, hard to escape.

f.g: A narrow well shaft—once in, hard to climb out.

chapters.n: She lies in wait like a robber and multiplies the unfaithful among men.

f.w: lieth in wait as for a prey

chapters.n: A series of questions builds a portrait: who has misery, fights, complaints, unexplained bruises, and bloodshot eyes?

f.g: Bloodshot or dull eyes from drinking.
Complaining, endless talk.

chapters.n: The answer: those who linger over wine and keep going after mixed drinks.

f.g: Wine mixed with spices to make it stronger.
tarry = linger, stay long.

chapters.n: Don’t gaze at wine when it sparkles red in the cup and goes down smoothly. Temptation often starts with looking.

f.g: When it goes down smoothly.

f.w: Look not thou upon the wine

chapters.n: In the end it bites like a snake and poisons like a viper.

f.g: adder = a venomous snake, a viper.

chapters.n: Under the influence, your eyes will see strange things and your mind will speak nonsense—or, as some read it, you’ll look at other women.

f.g: Hebrew can mean “strange things” (hallucinations) or “strange women.”

chapters.n: The drunk feels like someone lying in the middle of the sea or perched atop a ship’s swaying mast—dizzy and unstable.

f.w: upon the top of a mast
f.g: A picture of the dizzy swaying of drunkenness.

chapters.n: The final, sad words of the drunk: “They hit me, but I felt nothing. When will I wake up? I’ll go get another drink.” A vivid picture of addiction.

f.w: I will seek it yet again

chapters.n: Don’t envy wicked people or want to hang out with them.

f.w: Be not thou envious against evil men

chapters.n: Their hearts plot violence and their lips talk about causing trouble.

f.g: Plans violence.

chapters.n: A household—a family and a life—is built by wisdom and made secure by understanding.

f.w: Through wisdom is an house builded

chapters.n: Knowledge fills its rooms with rare and beautiful treasures. A wise home is rich in more than possessions.

f.g: chambers = rooms.

chapters.n: Wisdom is a kind of strength; knowledge increases power.
Wage war with careful strategy; many advisers bring victory.

f.w: in multitude of counsellors there is safety

chapters.n: Wisdom is out of a fool’s reach; he has nothing to say when serious matters are discussed at the city gate.

f.g: Where elders met to decide community matters.

chapters.n: Whoever plans evil will be known as a schemer.

f.g: Literally “master of schemes”—a known plotter.

chapters.n: Scheming folly is sin, and people detest a mocker.

f.w: The thought of foolishness is sin

chapters.n: If you give up when trouble comes, your strength is small. Hard times reveal real strength. (A play on words in Hebrew: “trouble” and “small” sound alike.)

f.w: If thou faint in the day of adversity

chapters.n: Rescue people being led away to death; don’t hold back from saving those stumbling toward slaughter.

f.g: forbear = hold back, refrain.

f.w: deliver them that are drawn unto death

chapters.n: If you claim, “We didn’t know,” the God who weighs hearts knows better. He sees what we could have done and will repay everyone by their works.

f.w: render to every man according to his works

chapters.n: Eat honey, my child, because it is good and sweet.
Wisdom is sweet like honey to your soul. Find it, and your future is secure and your hope will not be disappointed.

f.w: thy expectation shall not be cut off

chapters.n: A warning to the wicked: don’t ambush the home of the righteous or raid their dwelling.

f.g: Don’t destroy his home.

chapters.n: The righteous may fall many times, but they get back up; the wicked are brought down by disaster. Resilience, not perfection, marks the righteous—a comforting verse about repentance and perseverance.

f.w: a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again

chapters.n: Don’t gloat when your enemy falls or rejoice when he stumbles.

f.w: Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth

chapters.n: The Lord might be displeased and turn his anger from your enemy—to you. Gloating is itself a sin.
Don’t fret over evildoers or envy the wicked.

f.w: Fret not thyself because of evil men

chapters.n: The evil have no future; their lamp will be snuffed out.

f.w: the candle of the wicked shall be put out
f.g: candle = lamp.

chapters.n: Revere the Lord and the king, and don’t join rebels.

f.w: fear thou the LORD and the king
them that are given to change
f.g: Those who are rebellious or revolutionary.

chapters.n: Disaster from both will come suddenly—who knows what ruin they can bring? This ends the “words of the wise” section.

f.g: calamity = sudden disaster.

chapters.n: A short appendix begins: more sayings of the wise. Showing favoritism in court is wrong.

f.w: These things also belong to the wise
f.g: A heading for an added collection (24:23–34).
Partiality, favoritism.

chapters.n: A judge who tells the guilty “you’re innocent” will be cursed by people and hated by nations.
But those who convict the guilty will be blessed and things will go well for them.

f.g: Those who rightly convict the guilty.

chapters.n: An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips—a sign of true friendship.

f.g: A gesture of affection and loyalty.

chapters.n: Get your fields ready and your income secure, then build your house. Do first things first—sound advice for planning a life or a family.
Don’t testify against your neighbor without reason or use your words to deceive.

f.w: Be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause

chapters.n: Don’t say, “I’ll pay him back for what he did.” Revenge is forbidden; leave it to God.

f.w: I will do so to him as he hath done to me

chapters.n: A short story: the teacher passes the field and vineyard of a lazy man with no sense.

f.g: Lacking heart—without sense.

chapters.n: It is overgrown with thorns and weeds, and its stone wall has collapsed. Neglect slowly ruins what could be fruitful.

f.g: nettles = stinging weeds.

chapters.n: He looked closely, thought it over, and learned a lesson. Wisdom learns from observing life.

f.g: Learned a lesson.

chapters.n: The lazy man’s motto: just a little more sleep. (Repeats 6:10.)

f.w: a little folding of the hands

chapters.n: Poverty comes like a robber and scarcity like an armed soldier. (Repeats 6:11.) Small habits of neglect lead to big losses.

f.g: Like a vagabond or bandit.

chapters.n: A new collection (chapters 25–29): proverbs of Solomon copied by scholars in King Hezekiah’s court, about 250 years after Solomon. Hezekiah was a reforming king who valued Israel’s heritage.

f.g: Reigned about 715–686 BC; a righteous king of Judah.
Transcribed, collected, edited.

chapters.n: God’s glory includes mysteries beyond us; a king’s glory is to investigate matters carefully. God reveals in his time, and leaders must search diligently.

f.w: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing

chapters.n: Like the height of heaven and the depth of the earth, a king’s mind can’t be fully understood.

f.g: Beyond finding out.

chapters.n: Remove the impurities from silver, and a craftsman can make something beautiful.

f.g: dross = impurities skimmed off molten metal.
finer = refiner, silversmith.

chapters.n: Likewise, remove wicked advisers from the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.

f.w: his throne shall be established in righteousness

chapters.n: Don’t push yourself forward in the king’s presence or claim a place among the great.

f.g: Don’t exalt yourself; don’t show off.

chapters.n: Better to be invited up than to be sent down in front of others. Jesus taught a parable about taking the lowest seat at a feast that echoes this.
Don’t rush to take someone to court; what will you do if your neighbor proves you wrong?

f.w: Go not forth hastily to strive

chapters.n: Settle your dispute privately with your neighbor, and don’t betray someone else’s confidence to win.

f.w: Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself

f.g: discover = reveal.

chapters.n: Otherwise people will shame you, and your bad reputation will never go away.

f.g: infamy = disgrace, bad reputation.

chapters.n: A word spoken at the right moment is like golden apples set in silver—beautiful and precious.

f.g: Silver settings, carvings, or filigree.

chapters.n: Wise correction given to a listening ear is as lovely as gold jewelry.

f.w: a wise reprover upon an obedient ear

chapters.n: A faithful messenger refreshes those who send him like cool snow-water at harvest time. (Snow from Mount Hermon may have been used to cool drinks.)

f.w: the cold of snow in the time of harvest
f.g: A cooling drink during the heat of harvest—refreshing, not snowfall itself.

chapters.n: Someone who boasts of gifts he never gives is like clouds and wind that bring no rain—full of promise, empty of help.
Patience can persuade a ruler, and a gentle tongue can break bone—softness can overcome the hardest resistance.

f.w: a soft tongue breaketh the bone

f.g: Patience, slowness to anger.

chapters.n: Found honey? Eat just enough, or you’ll get sick. Good things are best in moderation.

f.w: eat so much as is sufficient for thee

chapters.n: Don’t visit your neighbor too often, or he’ll grow tired of you. Even friendship needs balance.

f.g: Don’t set foot there too often.

chapters.n: A false witness is as deadly as a war club, a sword, or a sharp arrow.

f.g: maul = a heavy club or hammer used as a weapon.

chapters.n: Relying on an unreliable person in a crisis is like chewing with a broken tooth or walking on a sprained foot—painful and useless.

f.g: A lame or slipping foot.

chapters.n: Singing cheerful songs to a grieving person is like taking away their coat on a cold day or pouring vinegar on soda—it only stirs things up. Sensitivity matters more than cheerfulness.

f.g: nitre = soda (natron); vinegar on it fizzes violently.

chapters.n: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if thirsty, give him water. Paul quotes this, and Jesus taught to love our enemies.
Kindness may burn with shame in his conscience and lead him to change, and the Lord will reward you. The “coals of fire” likely refer to remorse, not harm.

f.w: heap coals of fire upon his head
f.g: Likely a figure of burning shame or repentance stirred by unexpected kindness.

chapters.n: As the north wind brings rain, a sly tongue brings angry looks. (Some read: an angry look stops gossip.)

f.g: backbiting = speaking evil of someone behind their back.

chapters.n: Repeats 21:9: better a corner of the roof than a big house shared with a quarrelsome spouse.
Good news from far away is as refreshing as cold water to someone parched—precious in a world of slow travel.

f.w: good news from a far country

chapters.n: A righteous person who caves in to the wicked is like a muddied spring or polluted well—something that should give life is spoiled.

f.g: A spring muddied by trampling feet.

chapters.n: Too much honey is bad, and seeking your own glory isn’t glorious.

f.w: for men to search their own glory is not glory

chapters.n: A person without self-control is like a city with broken-down walls—defenseless against every attack.

f.w: He that hath no rule over his own spirit

chapters.n: Verses 1–12 sketch the fool. Honor fits a fool about as well as snow in summer or rain at harvest—out of place and even harmful.

f.g: Rare in Israel’s dry summer and damaging to ripe grain.
seemly = fitting.

chapters.n: An undeserved curse is like a darting bird or swallow—it flutters about but never lands. Unjust curses have no power.

f.w: the curse causeless shall not come

chapters.n: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the fool—some only respond to force.

f.w: a rod for the fool's back

chapters.n: Don’t answer a fool on his own terms, or you’ll become just like him.

f.w: Answer not a fool according to his folly
f.g: Don’t sink to his level.

chapters.n: Yet sometimes you must answer a fool, or he’ll think he’s wise. Verses 4–5 placed side by side teach that wisdom knows when to answer and when to stay silent.

f.w: Answer a fool according to his folly
f.g: Expose his folly so he won’t be wise in his own eyes.
conceit = opinion, estimation.

chapters.n: Sending a message by a fool is like cutting off your own feet or drinking poison—you only hurt yourself.

f.g: Drinks down violence—brings harm on himself.

chapters.n: A proverb in a fool’s mouth is as useless as a lame man’s legs.

f.w: The legs of the lame are not equal
f.g: Or “hang limp,” useless.

chapters.n: Honoring a fool is like tying a stone into a sling—it won’t work and may backfire.

f.w: bindeth a stone in a sling
f.g: A stone tied in can’t be thrown; or it whips back and hurts the slinger.

chapters.n: A proverb in a fool’s mouth is like a thorn in a drunk’s hand—he doesn’t know how to use it and may hurt others.

f.w: a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard
f.g: A drunk waving a thornbush, harming himself and others.

chapters.n: A difficult verse with many readings. KJV: God, who made all, repays fools and sinners. Many modern versions: like an archer wounding at random is one who hires a fool or a passer-by.

f.w: The great God that formed all things
f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; it may mean “a master craftsman” or “an archer.”

chapters.n: A fool returns to his folly like a dog returns to its vomit. Peter quotes this about those who go back to sins they had left.

f.w: As a dog returneth to his vomit

chapters.n: There’s more hope for a fool than for someone who thinks he’s already wise. Pride is harder to fix than ignorance.
Verses 13–16 sketch the lazy person. His excuse: “There’s a lion in the road!”

f.w: There is a lion in the way

chapters.n: A comic picture: the lazy person turns on his bed like a door on its hinges—moving, but going nowhere.

f.w: As the door turneth upon his hinges
f.g: Lots of motion, no progress.

chapters.n: He buries his hand in the dish and is too tired to bring it back to his mouth. (See 19:24.)

f.g: It wears him out.

f.w: hideth his hand in his bosom
f.g: Better “buries his hand in the dish.”

chapters.n: The lazy person thinks he is wiser than seven people who can give sensible answers. Laziness often hides behind excuses that sound clever.

f.w: seven men that can render a reason
f.g: Seven = many; people who answer with good sense.

chapters.n: Meddling in someone else’s quarrel is like grabbing a stray dog by the ears—you’re asking to get bitten.

f.w: taketh a dog by the ears
f.g: Dogs were often wild scavengers, not pets.

chapters.n: Like a madman shooting flaming arrows and deadly darts…

f.g: firebrands = flaming arrows or burning sticks.

chapters.n: …so is someone who deceives his neighbor and then says, “I was only joking!” Harmful “jokes” do real damage.

f.g: “Wasn’t I just kidding?”

chapters.n: Without wood a fire goes out; without gossip, quarrels die down.

f.g: talebearer = gossip, whisperer.

chapters.n: As charcoal feeds embers and wood feeds fire, a quarrelsome person fuels conflict.

f.w: a contentious man to kindle strife

chapters.n: Gossip is like delicious morsels that sink deep inside. (Repeats 18:8.)

f.g: Likely “like delicious morsels.”

chapters.n: Smooth, fervent words hiding an evil heart are like a cheap clay pot coated with glaze—shiny outside, worthless inside.

f.w: a potsherd covered with silver dross
f.g: A clay pot coated with glaze or cheap silver slag.
Fervent, warm-sounding words.

chapters.n: A hateful person disguises it with his words while storing up deceit inside.

f.g: dissembleth = disguises, pretends.

chapters.n: When he speaks graciously, don’t trust him—his heart is full of evil.

f.g: Seven = completeness; his heart is full of evil.

chapters.n: His hatred may be hidden by deceit, but his wickedness will be exposed publicly.
Whoever digs a pit for others will fall into it; whoever rolls a stone will have it roll back on him.

f.w: Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein

chapters.n: A liar hates those he hurts, and flattery leads to ruin.
Don’t brag about tomorrow, because you don’t know what a day will bring. James teaches the same humility about our plans.

f.w: Boast not thyself of to morrow

chapters.n: Let others praise you, not your own mouth—a stranger, not your own lips.
Stones and sand are heavy, but the trouble a fool’s anger causes is heavier still.

f.g: His provocation, the vexation he causes.

chapters.n: Anger is cruel and fury overwhelming, but jealousy is even harder to withstand.

f.g: Or jealousy—a consuming passion.
outrageous = overflowing, like a flood.

chapters.n: Honest correction spoken openly is better than love that never shows itself.

f.w: Open rebuke is better than secret love

chapters.n: A friend’s honest words may hurt, but they can be trusted; an enemy’s kisses are fake. Think of Judas’s kiss.

f.w: Faithful are the wounds of a friend
the kisses of an enemy are deceitful

chapters.n: When you’re full, even honey is unappealing; when you’re hungry, even bitter food tastes sweet. Need changes how we value things.

f.g: loatheth = tramples on, refuses with disgust.

chapters.n: A person who wanders from home is like a bird that strays from its nest—vulnerable and restless.
Perfume and oil delight the heart, and so does a friend’s heartfelt advice.

f.g: Fragrant oils were used to refresh guests.
Advice that comes from the heart.

chapters.n: Don’t abandon old family friends. When trouble hits, a nearby neighbor may help more than a distant relative.

f.w: better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off

chapters.n: Be wise, my child, and make me glad, so I can answer anyone who criticizes me. A child’s good life vindicates the parent’s teaching.

f.g: Anyone who insults or criticizes me.

chapters.n: The prudent see danger and take refuge; the naive keep going and suffer. (Repeats 22:3.)

f.w: A prudent man foreseeth the evil

chapters.n: Take the coat of someone who guarantees a stranger’s debt. (Nearly repeats 20:16.)
A loud blessing shouted early in the morning will be taken as a curse. Overdone or badly timed praise can seem fake or annoying.

f.g: At an inconvenient hour, when people are still sleeping.

chapters.n: A quarrelsome spouse is like a constant drip on a rainy day.
Trying to restrain her is like trying to hold back the wind or grab oil with your hand.

f.g: bewrayeth = betrays, reveals; the oil can’t be grasped and gives itself away.

chapters.n: As iron sharpens iron, one person sharpens another. Good friends improve each other through honest interaction.

f.g: Face—here the whole person, their character.

chapters.n: Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever faithfully serves his master will be honored.

f.w: he that waiteth on his master shall be honoured

chapters.n: As water reflects a face, a person’s heart reflects who they really are—or, others can see themselves in us.

f.w: As in water face answereth to face
f.g: Like a reflection in still water.

chapters.n: Death and the grave are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes—we always want more.

f.g: Sheol and Abaddon—the grave and the place of destruction.

f.w: the eyes of man are never satisfied

chapters.n: As fire tests silver and gold, praise tests a person. How we handle praise reveals our character.

f.g: fining pot = a crucible for refining.

chapters.n: Even if you grind a fool like grain in a mortar, you won’t get the folly out of him. Stubborn folly resists even harsh measures.

f.g: bray = pound, crush.
A bowl where grain was pounded with a club (pestle).

chapters.n: Verses 23–27 are a short poem about farming. Know the condition of your flocks and pay attention to your herds.

f.g: Literally “the face of your flocks”—know each animal.

chapters.n: Riches don’t last forever, and even a crown doesn’t pass securely to every generation. Steady, careful stewardship matters more.
When the hay is cut and new growth appears, and the hillside grasses are gathered, God’s provision shows itself.

f.g: Grasses and plants gathered from the hillsides.

chapters.n: Lambs provide wool for clothing, and goats can be sold to buy a field.

f.g: Goats can be sold to buy land.

chapters.n: There will be plenty of goat’s milk for your family and your servants. Faithful stewardship of what you have leads to lasting provision.

f.g: maidens = female servants.

chapters.n: A guilty conscience makes the wicked run even when no one is chasing them; the righteous are bold as lions.

f.w: The wicked flee when no man pursueth

chapters.n: When a nation rebels, rulers come and go quickly; a wise, discerning leader brings lasting stability. Northern Israel’s many short-lived kings illustrate this.
A poor person who oppresses other poor people is like a driving rain that washes away crops instead of watering them.

f.w: a sweeping rain which leaveth no food
f.g: A torrential storm that flattens and destroys crops.

chapters.n: Abandoning God’s law leads people to praise the wicked; keeping it leads people to oppose them.
Evil people don’t understand justice, but those who seek the Lord understand it fully. Spiritual understanding comes from seeking God.

f.w: they that seek the LORD understand all things

chapters.n: Better to be poor and live with integrity than to be rich and crooked.

f.w: Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness

chapters.n: A child who keeps God’s law is wise; one who hangs out with gluttons shames his father.

f.g: Gluttons, wasteful partiers.

chapters.n: Wealth gained by charging the poor excessive interest will end up with someone who is kind to the poor.

f.g: usury = interest; Israel’s law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite.

chapters.n: If someone refuses to listen to God’s law, even their prayers are detestable. God hears those who are willing to hear him.

f.w: even his prayer shall be abomination

chapters.n: Whoever leads the upright astray will fall into his own trap, but the blameless will inherit good things.

f.w: causeth the righteous to go astray

chapters.n: The rich may think themselves wise, but a poor person with insight can see right through them.

f.g: Sees through him, exposes him.

chapters.n: When the righteous triumph, there is great celebration; when the wicked rise to power, people go into hiding.
Hiding sins leads nowhere good, but confessing and abandoning them brings mercy. A key verse on repentance.

f.w: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper

chapters.n: Blessed is the one who always reveres God, but whoever hardens their heart falls into trouble.

f.g: Always stays reverent and careful before God.

chapters.n: A wicked ruler over poor people is like a roaring lion or a charging bear.

f.g: A charging, rampaging bear.

chapters.n: A ruler without understanding is a cruel oppressor; one who hates dishonest gain will reign a long time.

f.g: covetousness = greed for unjust gain.

chapters.n: A murderer, tormented by guilt, is a fugitive until death; let no one help him escape.

f.g: Let no one hold him back or support him.

chapters.n: Whoever walks with integrity will be kept safe; whoever is crooked will suddenly fall.

f.w: Whoso walketh uprightly shall be saved

chapters.n: Working your land brings plenty of food; chasing fantasies brings plenty of poverty. (Nearly repeats 12:11.)

f.g: Or “worthless pursuits.”

chapters.n: A faithful person will be richly blessed, but one eager to get rich quick won’t stay innocent.

f.w: he that maketh haste to be rich

chapters.n: Showing favoritism is wrong—yet some will do wrong for just a piece of bread. Partiality can be bought cheaply.

f.g: Partiality, favoritism.

chapters.n: The stingy hurry to get rich, not realizing poverty is coming.

f.g: A stingy, greedy outlook.

chapters.n: Whoever corrects someone will in the end gain more favor than one who flatters.

f.w: He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour

chapters.n: Whoever robs his own parents and says, “It’s not wrong,” is no better than a vandal.

f.w: Whoso robbeth his father or his mother

chapters.n: A greedy, arrogant person stirs up conflict; whoever trusts the Lord will prosper.

f.g: Literally “a wide soul”—greedy, grasping.
Prospered, enriched.

chapters.n: Trusting only your own mind is foolish; walking in wisdom keeps you safe.

f.w: He that trusteth in his own heart is a fool

chapters.n: Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing, but whoever looks away from them will receive many curses.

f.w: He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack

f.g: Looks away from need on purpose.

chapters.n: When the wicked rise to power, people go into hiding; when they perish, the righteous flourish.
Someone who stays stubborn after repeated correction will suddenly be broken beyond repair.

f.g: Becomes stiff-necked—like an ox refusing the yoke.

chapters.n: When the righteous lead, the people rejoice; when the wicked rule, the people groan. The Book of Mormon’s King Mosiah taught this same truth about government.

f.w: When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice

chapters.n: A child who loves wisdom makes the father glad; one who keeps company with prostitutes wastes his wealth—like the prodigal son.
A king who rules with justice stabilizes a land; one who demands bribes or heavy taxes tears it down.

f.g: One who takes bribes, or a man of heavy levies.

chapters.n: Flattering a neighbor is like spreading a net for his feet—it sets him up to fall.
Evildoers are trapped by their own sin, but the righteous sing and rejoice.
The righteous care about justice for the poor; the wicked don’t even want to know.

f.w: considereth the cause of the poor

chapters.n: Mockers stir up a whole city, but the wise calm the anger.

f.w: bring a city into a snare
f.g: Set a city aflame with unrest.

chapters.n: When a wise person takes a fool to court, the fool only rages or laughs, and there’s no peace. Some disputes can’t be won.
The bloodthirsty hate people of integrity, but the upright care for their lives.

f.g: Seek to protect his life.

chapters.n: A fool vents all his anger, but a wise person quietly holds it back.

f.w: A fool uttereth all his mind
f.g: mind = spirit, temper—he lets it all out.

chapters.n: If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will become corrupt. Leaders set the tone for those under them.
The poor and their oppressor have this in common: the Lord gives light to the eyes of both. God gives life to all.

f.w: the LORD lighteneth both their eyes

f.g: The oppressor.

chapters.n: A king who judges the poor fairly will have a throne established forever.

f.w: his throne shall be established for ever

chapters.n: Discipline and correction impart wisdom; a child left without guidance brings shame to his mother.

f.g: Left without guidance or boundaries.

chapters.n: When the wicked increase, so does sin—but the righteous will see their downfall.

f.w: the righteous shall see their fall

chapters.n: Discipline your child, and he will give you peace and delight.
Where there is no revelation from God, people run wild; blessed is the one who keeps God’s law. “Vision” here means prophetic revelation, not just planning.

f.w: Where there is no vision, the people perish
f.g: vision = prophetic revelation; perish = cast off restraint, run wild.

f.w: he that keepeth the law, happy is he

chapters.n: A servant can’t be corrected by words alone; even if he understands, he won’t respond.

f.g: He won’t respond or obey.

chapters.n: There’s more hope for a fool than for someone who speaks rashly.
A servant pampered from childhood may in the end become insolent or claim to be family. The Hebrew of the last word is uncertain.

f.g: Pampers, spoils.
The Hebrew word is rare; it may mean “heir” or “trouble.”

chapters.n: An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered one commits many sins.

f.w: An angry man stirreth up strife

chapters.n: Pride brings a person low, but the humble in spirit gain honor.

f.w: A man's pride shall bring him low

chapters.n: An accomplice to a thief harms himself: he hears the oath to testify but stays silent. Covering for wrongdoing makes you guilty too.

f.g: He hears the curse placed on anyone who withholds testimony.
bewrayeth = reveals, discloses.

chapters.n: Fear of what people think is a trap, but trusting the Lord keeps you safe.

f.w: The fear of man bringeth a snare

chapters.n: Many seek favor from rulers, but true justice comes from the Lord.

f.w: every man's judgment cometh from the LORD

chapters.n: The righteous detest the dishonest, and the wicked detest the upright. The Hezekiah collection ends with the two ways in clear contrast.

f.g: abomination = something detestable.

chapters.n: A new collection: the words of Agur son of Jakeh. Nothing else is known of him; some Jewish tradition took “Agur” as a pen name for Solomon, while many scholars think he was a non-Israelite sage. Ithiel and Ucal may be students—or the Hebrew may be read as a lament, “I am weary, O God.”

f.g: Otherwise unknown; possibly from Massa, a north Arabian people (see the word “prophecy,” which can be read as “of Massa”).
Hebrew massa—an oracle or burden; possibly a place name.

chapters.n: Agur begins with deep humility: compared to God’s wisdom, he feels as dull as an animal. True wisdom begins by admitting how little we know.

f.g: brutish = stupid, like a beast.

f.w: Surely I am more brutish than any man

chapters.n: He confesses he hasn’t mastered wisdom or knowledge of the Holy One.

f.g: Knowledge of the Holy One—God.

chapters.n: A series of questions like those God asked Job: who goes up to heaven and comes down? who holds the wind and the waters? Only God. “What is his son’s name?” Christians have long heard here a hint of the Son of God, who came down from heaven.

f.w: Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended?

chapters.n: God’s every word is pure, tested like refined metal, and he shields those who trust him. Answers to life’s deep questions come from God’s revealed word.

f.w: Every word of God is pure

f.g: Refined, tested in fire like precious metal.

chapters.n: Don’t add your own ideas to God’s words, or he will rebuke you and expose you as a liar. Latter-day Saints understand this as a warning against human tampering, not against God himself giving further revelation.

f.w: Add thou not unto his words

chapters.n: Agur prays for two things before he dies—the only prayer in Proverbs.

f.w: Two things have I required of thee
f.g: required = asked, requested.

chapters.n: First, keep me from falsehood and lies. Second, give me neither poverty nor riches—just the daily bread I need. Jesus taught a similar request in the Lord’s Prayer.

f.w: give me neither poverty nor riches

f.g: convenient = needful, my allotted portion.

chapters.n: Why? If I have too much, I may forget God and say, “Who is the Lord?” If too little, I may steal and dishonor his name. Both extremes are spiritual dangers.

f.w: Lest I be full, and deny thee
take the name of my God in vain

chapters.n: Don’t slander a servant to his master, or he’ll curse you and you’ll be held guilty. Protect those with little power.

f.w: Accuse not a servant unto his master

chapters.n: Verses 11–14 describe four kinds of corrupt people (“a generation” here means a type of person). First: those who curse their parents.
Second: those who think they are pure but haven’t been washed from their filth—self-righteousness.
Third: those with haughty eyes and arrogant looks.
Fourth: those whose teeth are like swords and knives, devouring the poor and needy. Greed is pictured as a ravenous animal.

f.w: to devour the poor from off the earth

chapters.n: Agur uses number sayings (“three… yea, four”). The leech has two daughters named “Give! Give!”—a picture of insatiable greed. Four things are never satisfied.

f.g: horseleach = leech, a bloodsucking worm.

f.w: three things that are never satisfied
f.g: The “three… yea, four” pattern builds to the last item for emphasis.

chapters.n: The four never-satisfied things: the grave, a barren womb longing for a child, dry ground thirsting for water, and fire always wanting more fuel.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the realm of the dead, which always takes more.

chapters.n: A grim image: the eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother will be pecked out by ravens and eaten by vultures—an unburied, shameful death.

f.g: Likely vultures, which eat carrion.

chapters.n: Agur names three—yea, four—things too wonderful for him to understand.
An eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, a ship at sea, and a man with a young woman. Each leaves no trail and moves in mysterious ways—love between a man and woman is a wonder.

f.w: the way of a man with a maid
f.g: maid = a young woman; the mystery of love and attraction.

chapters.n: By contrast, the adulteress treats sin like a snack: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, “I’ve done nothing wrong.” She feels no shame.

f.g: Acts as if nothing happened.

chapters.n: Four things make the earth tremble because they turn the normal order upside down.

f.g: disquieted = shaken, troubled.

chapters.n: A servant who suddenly becomes king, and a fool who is stuffed with food—both often abuse their new position.
An unloved woman who finally gets married, and a maidservant who replaces her mistress—both may become proud or harsh. Hagar and Sarah show the tension.

f.w: an handmaid that is heir to her mistress

f.g: odious = hated, unloved.

chapters.n: Four small creatures teach big lessons in wisdom.

f.g: Wise beyond their size—skillful by instinct.

chapters.n: Ants are weak, yet they store food in summer. Planning ahead makes up for weakness.
Rock badgers are weak, yet they live safely among the rocks. Knowing where to find refuge is wise. Scripture often calls the Lord a rock.

f.g: Rock hyraxes—small, rabbit-sized animals that live in rocky crags.

chapters.n: Locusts have no king, yet they advance in orderly ranks. Unity and cooperation give strength.

f.g: In ranks, in divisions, like an army.

chapters.n: A lizard (KJV “spider”) can be caught by hand, yet it lives in royal palaces. Small and ordinary, it gets into the highest places.

f.g: Hebrew semamit, probably a gecko or lizard.

chapters.n: Four things move with stately dignity.

f.g: Graceful, dignified in their stride.

chapters.n: The lion, mightiest of beasts, who backs down from nothing.
A strutting rooster or greyhound (the Hebrew is unclear), a male goat leading the flock, and a king with his army around him.

f.g: Hebrew uncertain—possibly a strutting rooster or a war horse.

f.w: against whom there is no rising up
f.g: Possibly “with his army around him.”

chapters.n: If you’ve foolishly exalted yourself or plotted evil, clap your hand over your mouth—stop before it goes further.

f.w: lay thine hand upon thy mouth

chapters.n: Churning milk produces butter, twisting a nose produces blood, and stirring up anger produces conflict. In Hebrew, “nose” and “anger” are the same word—a clever wordplay.

f.g: Hebrew ʾaf means both “nose” and “anger.”

f.w: the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife

chapters.n: The final collection: words of King Lemuel, taught to him by his mother. Lemuel is otherwise unknown (some Jewish tradition identified him with Solomon). It is remarkable that a mother’s teaching closes the book.

f.g: “Lemuel” means “belonging to God.” Nothing else is known of him.

f.w: the prophecy that his mother taught him
f.g: Possibly “king of Massa.”

chapters.n: His mother speaks with deep emotion: “What, my son? Son of my womb? Son of my vows?” She may have dedicated him to God in prayer, like Hannah with Samuel.
Her first warning: don’t waste your strength on many women or on the things that ruin kings. Solomon’s many wives turned his heart away.
Second: kings shouldn’t drink wine, nor rulers crave strong drink.

f.w: it is not for kings to drink wine

chapters.n: Drinking makes rulers forget the law and deny justice to the vulnerable. Leaders need a clear mind.
Strong drink was used as a sedative for the dying or those in deep grief—a kind of ancient painkiller, not a pastime.

f.w: him that is ready to perish

chapters.n: Let the suffering forget their misery for a while. The contrast stresses that a king has no such excuse.

f.g: A concession to the suffering, not an endorsement of drinking.

chapters.n: Third: speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves—the defenseless and those facing ruin.

f.w: Open thy mouth for the dumb
f.g: dumb = unable to speak; here, those with no voice in society.

chapters.n: Judge fairly and defend the rights of the poor and needy. This is the true calling of leadership.

f.w: plead the cause of the poor and needy

chapters.n: The book closes with a 22-verse poem praising a woman of strength. In Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet (an acrostic)—a complete A-to-Z of wisdom in action.

f.g: Hebrew ʾeshet ḥayil—a woman of strength, valor, and capability; used of Ruth.

f.w: her price is far above rubies

chapters.n: Her husband trusts her completely, and he never lacks what he needs.

f.g: spoil = gain, plunder; he lacks nothing of value.

chapters.n: She brings him good, not harm, every day of her life.

f.w: all the days of her life

chapters.n: She chooses wool and flax and works eagerly with her hands.

f.g: A plant whose fibers were spun into linen.

chapters.n: Like a merchant ship, she brings provisions from far away—she is resourceful and enterprising.

f.g: Trading ships that brought goods from distant ports.

chapters.n: She gets up before dawn to feed her household and plan the work for her servants.

f.g: Assigns tasks, or food, to her servant girls.

chapters.n: She evaluates a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard. She is a capable businesswoman.

f.w: She considereth a field, and buyeth it
f.g: considereth = examines carefully, evaluates.

chapters.n: She works vigorously and strengthens her arms for the tasks ahead.

f.w: She girdeth her loins with strength
f.g: Ties up her robe for action—gets ready to work hard.

chapters.n: She sees that her trading is profitable, and her lamp burns late into the night.

f.w: her candle goeth not out by night
f.g: candle = lamp; she works late, or her home is never without light.

chapters.n: She spins thread with her own hands.

f.g: A rod used for twisting fibers into thread.
A staff that holds unspun wool or flax.

chapters.n: Her hands that spin (v. 19) also reach out to the poor. Her industry serves charity, not only her own home.

f.w: She stretcheth out her hand to the poor

chapters.n: She doesn’t fear winter for her family, because they are all warmly clothed in fine scarlet garments.

f.g: Fine, costly, dyed wool—possibly “double garments” for warmth.

chapters.n: She makes her own bedspreads, and her clothing is fine linen and purple—a sign of dignity and prosperity.

f.g: Fine linen and purple-dyed cloth; purple dye was very expensive.
Embroidered coverlets or bedspreads.

chapters.n: Her husband is respected at the city gate, where he sits among the elders. Her excellence supports his good name.

f.g: The gate was where community leaders met and judged.

chapters.n: She makes linen garments and sashes and sells them to merchants.

f.g: girdles = sashes, belts.

chapters.n: She is clothed in strength and dignity and laughs without fear at the days ahead.

f.w: she shall rejoice in time to come
f.g: She laughs at the future—she is ready for it.

chapters.n: When she speaks, it is with wisdom, and kind teaching is on her tongue.

f.g: Teaching marked by ḥesed—loyal, faithful love.

chapters.n: She watches over the affairs of her household and is never idle.
Her children rise up and call her blessed, and her husband praises her too. Her family is her greatest tribute.

f.w: Her children arise up, and call her blessed

chapters.n: Her husband’s praise: “Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all.”
The poem’s heart: charm can deceive and beauty fades, but a woman who reveres the Lord deserves praise. The book ends where it began—with the fear of the Lord.

f.w: a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised

f.g: vain = fleeting, a passing breath.

chapters.n: Give her the reward she has earned, and let her deeds bring her praise in the city gates. Wisdom, personified as a woman in chapters 1–9, is here seen lived out in a real life.

f.w: let her own works praise her in the gates
